entries.label: The Warm Furrow
entries.text: Dawn smelled of frost and wet fur. Boof put her nose to the ground and read the field the way she read it every morning: loam-dark under the rime, burr-rough along the fence-foot. Everything was where it belonged. The latch lifted at the kitchen. The bucket knocked the well. A blackbird tried the same few notes until one pleased it. Beneath the berry rows, the torch-ants kept their little hearths, and their patient magic warmed the roots through winter; above them, the boonberries slept under ice, each holding a drop of light. What light they let slip ran downhill with the meltwater to the miller's pond, which is why that pond never freezes quite dark. On the coldest nights, when the frost split a furrow, you could see the hearths at work: a pin of light no bigger than a seed, carried down along a root by something with more legs than Boof cared to count, and behind it another, and another, a whole small procession going home along streets no map had room for. Boof did not dig. Some business is not a dog's, and the ants had never once asked her for anything. Torch-ants were businesslike, and very particular about torches. If one went out at the wrong corner, the whole street stopped until it was relit from the right one. Children lay with an ear to the frost to hear them keeping their corners: a dry, small ticking, like seeds in a gourd. Boof followed the rows past the fence that leaned into last year's weeds, past the scraping-post where the miller knocked the loam off his boots. She sniffed a root here and there, and the field gave back its usual answers: vole, frost-bitten clover, the sour ghost of a fox who had thought better of it. Boof knew this field. She worked for the land, wherever the fences stood. Nobody paid her, and nobody had needed to; the land kept her the way it kept the ants, without either side signing anything. She did not especially like blueberries. She appreciated them, which is a different thing, and which the field seemed to know. She sniffed. Stepped. Stopped. One furrow was warm. Too warm. Beneath it, the ants had stopped working. Or not stopped — gathered, the way they gather at a hearth when a new coal is laid. Boof dug. First frost, then soft earth, then a little cloud of steam. At the bottom lay an egg the size of a curled cat, dark as an old lamp. She touched it with one paw. It hummed. The steam climbed past her ears, met the cold, and came down as snow that did not sting, because it was warm. Children have a name for warm snow, and a way of making it they explain only to other children: a hearth-drift. Nobody had taught the field how. Down the walls of the hole, the torch-ants were already at their business. Her digging had cut one of their streets clean through. They did not complain; they carried their torches around the break in single file, a detour of pinpricks bending across the shell. One stopped and held its torch against the egg, the way a lamplighter tests a wick, then went back down a shade brighter. No nest. No tracks. No mother-scent. She went around the hole once more, slowly. Whatever had brought it here had left no way to follow. Inside the shell, an unspent wish waited. Boof heard only the hum.

entries.label: Boof · Ant-warmth smelled earthy and…
entries.text: Ant-warmth smelled earthy and even, like bread left under a cloth. This was sharper. A candle just blown out. Boof knew the paths to the kitchens, the mill with its flour-pale doorstep, and the grove nobody liked to name after dark; after supper people said the downhill trees, as if the grove might hear its name and come up to see what was wanted. She had never found an egg on any of them. Certainly not one that warmed a whole furrow. She rested her chin on the rim of the hole. The egg hummed against the earth. Under her chin, she felt it answer. She would have preferred a trail. Trails usually ended with something you could eat: a dropped crust, a vole, once a whole wheel of cheese gone into the ditch to think things over.

entries.label: When a Berry Remembers
entries.text: Every boonberry had been a blueberry once. A wish had passed over it on the way to being granted, leaving a little of its light behind. Most slept through everything: snow, crows, harvest. The town used them for supper and lanterns: berry-lamps in jam jars on the porch posts, crust-gold pies at harvest. Nobody ate one warm. By the time a boonberry reached a table it had given its light to a lamp or a pie, and what was left was sweet and ordinary. Boof had never wondered what the light was for. She had been busy. The berry nearest the egg shed its frost. A gold seam opened in its skin with a small sound, like a thumbnail on a jar lid. Its light leaned toward the shell, then past it, down the slope. The next berry turned. Then the next. Frost slid off the leaves in glass-clear sheets and broke on the furrows like a tray of cups set down too fast. Row by row, a low glow led toward the grove. Boof followed with her nose. The berries remembered this hum. Long ago, it had passed them going the other way. Boof put her nose to the nearest berry, and it told her something. It did not speak; it was more as if she remembered being told. Trees. The sack warm against her ribs. A long note out of the dark, rather pleased with itself. Nothing in it was wrong. Then it was a cold berry with a gold seam, and she could not have said whether it had shown her what was coming or reminded her of something that already had. Boonberries only ever foresee kindly, the field-hands say. Whether kind things are all they can see, or all they will tell, nobody has thought to ask them. She looked back at the hole. Something had come home. Why had nobody come to fetch it?

entries.label: The Maps That Look Away
entries.text: Before the frost was off the fences, Boof had carried the egg to the map-house in an old feed-sack. It was warm as a loaf and considerably heavier. She set it on the reading table. The archivist fetched a book. The map-house smelled of oak-gall ink and cold slate. Along the back wall ran the drying-line, where new maps hung by their corners like washing over a slate trough. In a loaf-wide gap between rolled maps in the rafters, a young shelf-owl sat as if it had been shelved there. Along a fold in the map, two roads touched. Boof knew those roads. A day's walk lay between them. Outside, a cart bell rang beneath the window. The archivist smoothed the fold. The bell dwindled to a far, thin chime. “Leave room for the path,” he murmured, to the map or to the bell, and did not say which path. Boof lifted her head. The archivist put a press-stone on the crease. Neither looked away first. His press-stones sat along the table's lip, river-flat, six in a rack cut for seven. One is always missing; it is the first thing an apprentice learns and the last thing anybody finds. Then he tried to enter the egg in the book. First, as archivists do, he pencilled it small in the margin in the makers' old shorthand, to see whether it would bear ink: .[egg], a thing that stays where it is put. The pencil skidded. He rubbed it out and tried ~[egg], a thing still on its way. That one held, faint as a hair. So he dipped the pen. Egg, one. Dawnward field. Unclaimed. The ink gathered into beads and rolled off the page. He tried a second pen, and then the good steel nib he kept for boundary disputes. Boof waited. Maps keep what has happened. An unspent wish has not happened yet, and the page had nowhere to put it. At last he pegged the page on the drying-line, since a stubborn entry sometimes sets when nobody is watching. The beads ran down and dropped into the trough until the page hung clean as a washed collar, all but the pencilled tilde. Below, the ink sat in one black drop and would not mix with the water. He unpegged the page and laid it in the book beside the old field map: an ordinary field, in some long-dead surveyor's brown ink. “First ink stays,” he said. Nobody scrapes the first hand on a map; whatever comes after goes in pencil beside it, so whoever opens the book next can see what changed, and what it changed from. Beside the ordinary field, faint as a hair, the tilde waited. The archivist wiped the table. Boof watched the stone. That, at least, he had known how to hold down.

entries.label: Following the Hum
entries.text: Outside, the berries still leaned toward the grove, every row combed one way like wet fur. Boof had spent the morning asking a book. The field had been pointing all along. She settled the feed-sack against her chest, where a pup might ride. A fine gold crack had opened at the egg's crown. It looked like a door left slightly ajar. The hum kept its steady measure. Her paws found another. Down the slope. Past the fogged cold-frames, past the last row, to the sloe hedge where the field gave up being a field. There she paused. Behind her stood a house full of maps. Ahead lay the way the berries remembered. In the hedge-bottom lay a scatter of baneberries, plum-black, a thorn on every stem, dropped where nobody picks. Boof smelled what they were saying before she reached them, cold and very sure of itself: that whoever carried a warm thing into the grove would come out without it. Baneberries tell you what will go wrong, the field-hands warn, and then it goes wrong because you were told. Boof put a paw on the nearest, the way the field-hands do, and leaned. It split with a small sour sound and said nothing more. She went ahead.

entries.label: Boof · Evening laid long light…
entries.text: Evening laid long light across the field. Boof was hungry; somewhere uphill a kitchen was frying onions, and the smell followed her like a dog that had not been told to stay. The egg was warm. For a while, that was all. Behind her, the berries glowed under their leaves. Ahead, the first trees crowded close. Then a sound came out of the grove. HONK. Long, bent, and rather pleased with itself. Like a goose that had learned jazz. Boof stopped with one paw raised. The egg's hum slipped into time with it. She had heard it once already, that morning, with her nose in a berry, and could not have said which time was the first. High over the treeline, nine geese crossed the last light in a ragged, swinging line and answered, each honk a little behind where a sensible goose would put it. Jazz-geese, people called that kind, and shut their windows. She waited for a second note from the grove. Leaves stirred. Nothing more. She put her paw down and entered the trees.

entries.label: A Beat Late
entries.text: By the second morning, warmth had worked through sack and strap and settled against Boof's ribs. Behind her, the town maps still showed an ordinary field. Ahead, the berries' remembered route ran into birch and fern and hazel-switch, where the air smelled damp—and somehow twice breathed. She stopped beneath the first tree. Nothing moved. Something arrived again. Boof had been here before. Not here exactly: at the end of a berry, in the field, for less time than a sniff. Trees. The sack warm against her ribs. Nothing wrong. Now it was all round her, real enough to sneeze at, and she could not tell whether the berry had seen it coming or the grove was only saying it back. In a place that answers a beat late, it is hard to be sure which came first. She decided, as dogs do, that it did not much matter, since nothing was wrong. She laid the egg on a mossy stone. Pollen hung in rings between the trunks, catching the light; her breath went out and came back thin, a little late. Then the hum returned. Again. Each time it carried something different: rain on leaves, the smell of supper, a door opening onto a morning she almost knew. The grove was trying out futures. None had happened yet. Boof listened until she could pick the returns apart. One came from the hollow cedar, low and round; another thinned among the birches; a third seemed to start behind her teeth. She closed her mouth. It came again. She tried the cedar first, nose leading. There was no second egg in the hollow. There was a wren, brown as a dropped glove and not much bigger than a walnut, sitting in a nest of shredded bark with its beak open, finishing the hum a beat after the egg had finished it. It looked at Boof as if she were the one who was late. Echo-wrens, the woodcutters called them; every hollow cedar kept a pair, and they sang everything a beat behind, axes included. At the grove's edge a wren-call meant anything that came back to you. Boof sneezed. Three cedars sneezed after her, politely, one at a time. The egg lay still on its stone, and the moss beneath it had begun to dry. She looked from that small pale patch to the trembling gold in the air. So much happening overhead, and down here one egg warming one stone. She kept a paw beside it, where she could feel which of them was real.

entries.label: Boof · The leaning berries had…
entries.text: The leaning berries had led her here—the grove beyond the last honest furrow, a place the town labeled as reserve growth and the workers called the listening thicket. Every step pressed an unfinished fragment out of the leaf-mold. Half a lullaby somebody stopped singing. The first word of a prayer nobody dared finish. A clerk saying no such entry , with the hollow confidence of someone who had never carried a wanting too small to say out loud. Boof knew how towns worked. When a record-house is too clean, the wanting does not vanish; it drains downhill into the wild growth, where nobody asks what you came for. This thicket was where Boon.land kept every wish it preferred not to admit to having, every note it wanted to sound and didn't. The same workers said, usually over a second cup of birch-sap tea, that hob-deer grazed in here: deer no taller than a boot, cropping the moss on days nobody keeps. Asked which days those were, they could never say, and took that as proof. Boof found one patch of moss cropped short and tidy. She had been fooled by rabbits before. Keep the morning, not the week, the workers say of dogs; nobody had thought to ask her which day this was.

entries.label: Boonberry · The berries here did…
entries.text: The berries here did not shine for the harvest. They were the wild cousins of the field rows: blueberries a wish had passed over long ago, each holding its drop of the granting. In the thicket they pulsed like grains under stress — bright when an echo rehearsed a future they remembered the taste of, dim when the thicket put them back to sleep. Their thorned runners hooked Boof's coat as she passed, like a shopkeeper with one more thing to show you. Boof recognized several of her own past silences reflected in the dark skins of the fruit—small wantings she had swallowed instead of sounding. That was the grove's first cruelty: it kept what the town preferred not to admit to. Unspent wants. Unsounded notes. And no torch-ants kept this ground. No lit streets ran along the roots; no small city held the winter off. Boof put her nose to a root out of habit and found it cold all the way down, like a house nobody has lived in for a winter. Torch-ants will not settle where a light comes back to them twice, the field-hands say; a torch that answers itself is a torch nobody can be particular about. So the wild rows grew cold and stubborn, living off whatever heat the echoes left behind, which was why their light flickered instead of holding.

entries.label: Echo · "Follow me," said an…
entries.text: "Follow me," said an echo that used Boof's own pitch from years earlier—the careful, hopeful voice she had used back when she still asked for things instead of working for them. The path forked around an ancient hollow cedar, loud with wrens, and rejoined on the other side. Time here did not reverse; it rehearsed. In the suspended dust of the pollen rings there was always a second egg, a breath behind the first, shivering in gold spores—the wish trying out a future where it had already been granted, then setting the future back down, unconvinced, and trying the next one.

entries.label: What the Echo Keeps
entries.text: Boof paced the fork, nose to moss, while the grove offered rain, harvest, a road back to a better morning. Each future fitted nearly. That was the trouble. The wish stayed warm through all of them, and the hum kept coming back for another try. She could spend her whole life here listening to almost. Try it again, a little changed: that is all the grove is doing, the woodcutters say, and they will not hear it called lying. They say it at the saw-pit too, to a cut that binds — back the blade out, set it a hair lower, keep the cut that runs. Boof had let a whole day of tries go by. Only one had held. It lay on the stone where she had put it, and the moss under it had dried pale. On her third pass, the moss beside her sank. Two prints, cloven and broad, pressed down a pace from her shoulder, then two more, walking away between the birches with nothing above them. The moss sighed up slowly behind each, like a cushion after a guest has gone. Boof put her nose in the nearest print and got nothing: no musk, no breath, no warm hide, not even the green of a crushed stem. A track without a scent was a word without a mouth. The woodcutters call it the lag-stag, and say it is white, though nobody has ever seen it, which is a bold thing to say about a colour. She followed the prints round the cedar and back. They came past her again, a beat late, and stopped beside the egg's stone, deep and square-set, as if something tall had stood there a moment, looking down. The moss rose. Nothing else did. Toward evening the light under the trees went moth-soft, and the rehearsal moths came off the bark, dusk moths the colour of old paper, to sun themselves on the warm shell. Their wings were smudged with weather: drizzle on one, a hard white glare like light off salt on another, and on the biggest, a grey-green storm sitting on a hill. The grove keeps its almanac on them. Woodcutters read the wings before felling, and are wrong about a third of the time, which is better than the almanac at the mill. Boof read only dust and lamp-oil, and the powder they left on the shell in the shape of tomorrow. She took up the sling. The moths lifted off one by one, a little put out. In the pollen, the other egg lingered a breath behind, then stayed where it was. Boof walked on. Downhill, damp bark gave way to salt air; under the sand, something older had begun to answer. She listened without turning back.

entries.label: The Fool · He leaned out of…
entries.text: Three wishes, says the old song. Wrong count, says the Fool. Three COMPLETED wishes — a wish isn't granted till it's finished. He leaned out of a cedar where no door had been cut, pollen on mismatched sleeves and cedar shavings in his collar, one hand cupped to his mouth like a brass bell. He'd been the honk in the treeline, of course. He sampled the trope the way you’d lift a plate off a stranger’s table. “You know this one: a lamp, a rub, three wishes, and a fool who wastes the third un-wishing the first.” Then he sounded it — HONK, one long bent note, which an echo-wren overhead tried a beat late and abandoned halfway — and handed it back changed: the song never counts the finishing. Anybody can start a wish. Starting is cheap. The grove is full of starts. What costs, what really costs, is the last word, said out loud, with your whole weight on it. Every trope you sample, he said, tipping an invisible hat to the egg, must be returned changed, with interest. Boof did not answer with a riddle, and she opened no book. She wrote the grove's first usable note on the air with her nose: an echo is a wish rehearsing; a rehearsal is not a granting; a granting needs a finisher. Then she trotted past him into the sand, because somewhere out there was whoever had left a wish one word short, and the trail smelled like the only honest question left.

entries.label: Boof · The grove fell away…
entries.text: The grove fell away behind her into a vast, wind-scoured plain of dry salt and baked earth, rime-white where the crust was thin. Boof stood at the edge of the Fool's Paradox . The crust forked and would not be two places at once. Under the rippled dunes, two older routes glowed like habits the land had never broken, both wanting the same next step—two directions of travel that had spent so many years almost meeting that they had worn a want of their own into the ground. Then the ground spoke under her pads: one long, low note, and every salt flake on the crust stood up and lay down again like the hair along a dog's back. Along one route the glow brightened and moved, slow as a barge, toward the seam, and stopped a whisker short. Along the other, something answered. Boof put her nose to a crack and smelled brine, old and cold: a sea that had moved downstairs. The salt-rakers at the edge of the flats called the crust the roof and the glowing routes the salt-whales' roads; on the roof, you did not stamp. Two whales, two roads, one turn, and neither in a hurry to give way. The egg against her ribs hummed louder whenever she faced the seam, the way a wish leans toward other unfinished things. Boof filed it where she filed everything, by nose, beside the ant-streets under the berry rows. The field had streets too small for any map, and the flats had roads too big for one, and both smelled of somebody patient going home. She was beginning to suspect the whole land was like that: kept by things too small or too slow to be asked, each one keeping something else. A leaning wooden signpost stood half-swallowed by drift-sand. Its painted lettering had flaked off seasons ago, but its long evening shadow stretched across the flats like an unyielding black needle. Around its foot lay a ring of flat black signal stones, set out so long ago the reason had worn off with the paint. Signal-skinks basked on every one, finger-long and salt-pale, tails busy as a clerk's pen. They flicked — short, short, long — and each stone answered with a faint tick of warmth. Nobody could read it. When Boof's shadow crossed the ring, every tail stopped mid-sentence and pointed down the signpost's shadow. At the tip of the shadow, right where the two routes wanted to become one turn, a curve of green glass broke the crust. Boof dug. The flats gave up a bottle, stoppered, sand-scoured, and warm in the way of a chair somebody has only just left.

entries.label: Paradox · The stopper turned. Steam…
entries.text: The stopper turned. Steam rose, folded, found sleeves. Out came the Off-Season Genie, neat as a handkerchief and dressed like a clerk on his first day without a desk, smelling faintly of tea and brass polish. He looked from egg to dog to glowing sand. “Two routes. One turn. Used to settle these before breakfast.” A wish, he explained, redirected what was already moving. These routes had been nearly meeting for a century. One coincidence and a Thursday would have done it. “Whales will wait for anything. It's the turn that won't.” He brushed his cuffs. “Of course, I'm closed.” The egg was the last unfinished wish from the practice he'd shut down; he recognized it at once and looked away a moment too late. Closed or not, he reached into the bottle's neck and drew out the bottle-desk. It came folded, the way a heron comes out of reeds: a leg, a hinge, another leg, a baize top no bigger than a tea-tray, pigeonholes, a dry inkwell. Its one drawer was labelled Thursdays. He opened it a finger's width, glanced in, and shut it before Boof's nose could count. What escaped smelled of rain on shop shutters and a fish supper eaten standing up. It was the most interesting thing he had shown her yet.

entries.label: The Fool · The Fool trotted backward…
entries.text: You know the trope: rub the lamp, mind the fine print. HONK. The fine print was never the trap. The wholesale price was. The Fool trotted backward down the dune, spinning an empty brass lamp on one finger, salt crusting the hems of his patchwork. He had sampled the old song of genies, and he handed it back changed. It was never three wishes and a catch, he honked. It was a price list all along, and the grand wishes were the loss leaders. Footprints filled with sand the moment his heels lifted.

entries.label: The Seam in the Sand
entries.text: The Genie set the desk square on the sand and laid his instruments out on its baize: the wish-scale, its brass pans balanced against coincidences instead of weights, each one stamped small; the resolution glass, long as a forearm, ground to show any want larger than a loaf; and the want-needle, quick to find a want. He had made emperors with these. Moved rivers. Unmade two emperors at cost. Boof sat still. The wish-scale stayed level. He set his lightest coincidence in the far pan, a met-on-the-stair no bigger than a lentil, and it sank with a clink, as if the question of her weighed nothing. Through the resolution glass she was a smudge with a field behind her, a crop in the field, a harvest in the crop. The glass, which could not see anything smaller than a loaf, saw everything around her and nothing of her. The want-needle circled, slowed, and tried again. “Below my resolution,” he said. “Emperors want loudly. Ants want small, but there are so many of them, all wanting the same warm inch, that it comes to a loud sound in the end. I did good business with ants. You appear to want—” He tapped the glass. “Something these don't show.” He cleaned the lens on his sleeve, although there was no dust on it. Boof waited with the patience she used beside a cupboard someone had forgotten opening. The needle caught a glint of evening, pointed briefly toward the bottle, then swung away. The Genie moved the bottle behind him. Neither mentioned it. Across the flats the wind brushed their footprints shallow, and the two old routes continued their long, unfinished turn. Far down the seam a whale groaned once, the way a sleeper complains about the blankets. For all his instruments, he had no measure for the length of this particular silence. Boof huffed and looked at the seam, where two old routes still leaned toward each other like tired dancers. Could he not simply grant the turn, seal the wish, mend the map? "I'm not saying no," said the Genie. "I'm saying reality is already moving very quickly in another direction, and every correction has to come out of somewhere. Perfect version costs a miracle. Mediocre version costs one coincidence and a Thursday. Your version—" and here his voice did something it had not done in years, which was lift "—I can't price your version. I can't even read it." A want too small for the instruments of empire. He had liquidated his whole practice without ever once seeing one. He had one thing left that was free, because he had never found a way to sell it. He gave it to her the way he used to give it to emperors at the door, after the bill: “Build where the land already leans. Never cut a road the land does not want.” The emperors had all gone off and cut roads anyway. Two of them he had later unmade, at cost. Boof looked at the seam.

entries.label: Boof · Boof huffed and walked…
entries.text: Boof huffed and walked between the routes, paws in the seam, her weight enough to give their leaning somewhere to go. Under her pads the crust shivered; far down, two long notes found each other. Behind her the two lines settled into one turn. A long-held chord came home. No miracle was billed. The Genie watched the dust settle over work he would have charged a Thursday for. On the signal stones every skink flicked at once — long, long, long — and every stone ticked warm, as if a message had waited a century to be sent. The Genie folded the bottle-desk back into its bottle, drawer last, without looking at the drawer. "I'm coming with you," he said, tucking the bottle under one arm. "Not to grant anything. Understand that. I am closed." But a want too small to read had just done, for free, what he would have billed a Thursday for, and a small want was the one wonder his price list had never carried. Ahead, where the desert gave way to saltbush and rising stone, Council Hill lifted its stormy silhouette against the evening sky, its storm grey-green, just as a moth had smudged it. The egg hummed against Boof's ribs, one word short of finished, and the three of them—dog, wish, and the only professional who had ever refused to guess it—walked toward the hill together.

entries.label: Boof · Council Hill kept a…
entries.text: Council Hill kept a great slab of split pine that refused to pick a side, and it was there, under crosswind weather, that Boof brought the egg to be argued over. She slipped beneath the trestle, chin on the timber, and found herself nose to frame with the Fool’s Mirror —an upright pane of polished weather that returned not your face but the exact shape of your wanting. The hill smelled of two weathers at once. Round the council ring stood seven posts, and on every post an iron weathercock, rust-red at the comb. They did not follow the wind. They turned toward whatever they favoured, and the wind followed them. The crosswind was only the weathercocks disagreeing, made weather. Twice in living memory all seven had agreed, and the hill went so still that papers stayed where they were put. Nobody remembered the vote. Everybody remembered the papers. At the head of the slab the crosswind loom worked without a weaver: dawn-wind for the warp, squall for the weft, the shuttle flying between them on its own. It wove the council's tablecloth an inch an hour, honey-gold and squall-teal, and when the vote turned, the weave changed colour. Cut into the slab's edge, at nose height, was the hill's first law: &[boon, bane]{table}. The founders had chiselled it in bracework before the first argument, the way a joiner writes a joint before she saws, so it could be leaned on and checked while tempers were cool. Two sides in one frame, merged without whitening either. One table round the lot, like a room you agree to stay in. Each delegate thumbed the braces before sitting, to be sure nobody had filed them open in the night. Nobody ever had. Boof sniffed the cut: resin and old thumbs. The ferry delegate thumbed it last, said “Two springs, one bed,” as if that were the whole of the law, and sat. Above her, the law of the hill was recited as it had been recited for generations: every permission in Boon.land is a key, iron or brass, and a key may be filed smaller in the open, before witnesses, with the shavings swept into the honest jar. A key may never be grown in secret. The jar had never once been emptied, which the hill considered the point. The Genie stood at the table's edge, hands folded, and added the one fact that mattered: a wish is the largest key ever cut. It opens the momentum of the world itself. That was when the bane-side chair creaked. The bitter pie arrived by hired cart, lattice crust tight over berries he'd kept too long. He offered nobody a slice. The wish, he proposed, should be valued, filed, and sold to someone prepared to bear its considerable responsibilities. He paused to let the council imagine such a person. Then supplied his own name. As the cart tipped, a berry worked loose from his lattice, plum-black with a thorn on its stem, and rolled across the pine to the youngest clerk's elbow. Boof smelled it before she saw it: cold, violet, a cellar smell, and under that something being said. On the hill they say a baneberry tells you what will go wrong, and that it goes wrong because you were told. The clerk heard, or thought he heard, that the wind would have his cap. So he took it off to keep it safe, and set it on the slab beside his chalk. Nothing is argued on the hill until it has been written. Write it before you argue it, the founders said, and cut their own law first to show how. So while the pie was still being reasonable, the youngest clerk chalked his motion on the pine beside the law: [wish]{BaneWAP}. A window, with one man's room round it, where the law had a table. Nobody needed to raise a voice. Boof sniffed both. The law smelled of resin. The motion smelled of chalk, which comes off. All round the ring the weathercocks swung: three to face the pie, three tails to him, the seventh spinning on its pin. The crosswind doubled, lifted the youngest clerk's cap off the slab where he had set it to keep it safe, and hung it in the gorse. Boof flattened her ears. She did not know how iron voted. She knew what it smelled like when it was cross.

entries.label: Mirror · The Fool’s Mirror shimmered…
entries.text: The Fool’s Mirror shimmered with the fury of the split sky. It whispered in a tone like wind through eaves: "What you see is not what is, but what your wanting is becoming." The delegates looked, one by one. The boon-side saw their small wants, snug as filed keys. Mr. BaneWAP looked longest, and the glass returned him honestly: every berry he had ever hoarded, pressed airless under crust, gone from sweet to bitter for want of being served. He was not a villain from elsewhere. He was the mirror of what wanting becomes when it stops handing out slices. The egg, reflected beside him, showed no bidder's number and no bounding box — a wish keeps its own law, and no appraisal on the hill could get purchase on its shell.

entries.label: The Fool · One-footed on the unsigned…
entries.text: Every court gets a vizier. I sampled that trope, folks — and honked it back as pastry. One-footed on the unsigned auction ledger, the Fool produced a small hot hand-pie from nowhere polite — clove and windfall apple — and set it before Mr. BaneWAP with a bow. The whisperer-at-the-throne, the schemer in the sleeve — an old trope, sampled a thousand times. He returned it changed, with interest: in Boon.land the vizier is baked goods, and you can smell exactly what he's been hoarding.

entries.label: No Key Covers the Egg
entries.text: Boof watched the argument cross the pine grain like weather. Boon and bane sat under one shared squall and bargained without declaring war; that was the table's whole genius. But when the clerks brought out the rack of civic keys — iron ones honestly narrowed, brass ones watched for secret growing — not one of them matched the egg. The youngest clerk carried the largest key to the key-file bench anyway and set it in the vise. He drew the file once, from habit, before remembering that the bench only makes keys smaller. He swept the grey filings into the honest jar and hung the key back, a hair lighter and no nearer. Blowing the last filings off his thumb, he said the register ought to have a box for what you do not know. Nobody wrote that down. The Genie explained it the way he priced everything, flatly and without pity: a wish is not property, because it is not a thing; it is a redirection of momentum the world already has. You cannot auction a bend in the river. You can only stand where it bends. From beneath the table, Boof could see the parts of the meeting the mirror missed: wet hems, hobnailed boots braced against the slope, a clerk warming cramped fingers under one arm. Whenever a delegate struck the pine, dust shook loose beside her nose. They wanted the rain kept off their roofs and the paths kept open to their doors; some wanted more, but those wants were there beneath the grander words. And she could see the tablecloth's hem, which showed her the vote before anyone above: teal when the bane-side spoke well, gold for the boon-side, and a muddy wet-straw weave whenever somebody spoke only to be heard. There was a good deal of wet straw. She shifted the egg away from a drip. Above her, someone asked who would be responsible for keeping it safe. None of the keys fitted. The oldest clerk tried the last one, set it down, and wrote: the wish stays with its finder. Round the ring the weathercocks came slowly to rest, every one pointing at the gap between the banners, which on Council Hill is how a tie is recorded. The youngest clerk wiped the pie's motion off the pine with his sleeve. “Chalk is cheaper than oak,” said a joiner on the bench, though the slab was pine. Rain ticked on the tabletop. Across it, the pie smiled. “And who,” he asked, “inherits from the finder?” Boof's fur lifted along her back. The clerk kept his pen above the page.

entries.label: Boof · Boof left the hill…
entries.text: Boof left the hill with the wish she had never asked to hold, down hill-slate steps dished by centuries of boots that had come down still disagreeing. Finder, the clerk had written, as if finding were a small thing a dog did with her nose and not a door the world had opened under her paws. The Genie walked beside her, unhurried. "He will not steal it," he said of the pie on the other road. "Stealing costs a miracle. Paperwork costs pocket change, and he knows which one he can afford." Behind them, at sundown, the clerks cut the day's end off the tablecloth and folded it for the shepherd whose roof had leaked worst that week: the one custom on the hill that has never needed a vote. Below the hill, two claims reached the hall of arches before supper. One named Boof. One called the wish an asset. The clerks pinned them side by side, shut the door, and went home. Under the desk, where no one thought to listen, the floor began to sing.

entries.label: Boof · The hall under the…
entries.text: The hall under the tall stone arches was calm the way a drawn bowstring is calm. Sunlight lay across cedar shelves and a long desk worn pale by elbows, and across the slate floor ran a hairline crack that hummed. Boof padded in on quiet paws, following the vibration before she could hear it — the Fool’s Song running the crack like a held breath. It was not only the crack that hummed. Down in the dark of it lived the hum-crickets, chalk-pale and no longer than a barleycorn, and they kept its pitch the way a choir keeps a note for a singer who has stepped out. The clerks fed them seed-cake crumbs at elevenses and crossed the floor in felt hush-slippers. A cricket that went silent, they said, meant somebody near the floor was lying. Two slips hung over the desk, pinned with silver bodkins, and both of them were pulling. One was the boon-claim: the wish belongs to whoever found it, and through her to everyone. The other had arrived at first light in Mr. BaneWAP's crust-brown envelope, sealed twice and smelling faintly of sour pastry: the wish is a thing, and things belong to whoever can hold them longest. Each slip leaned toward the egg in Boof's sling. The egg leaned toward neither. Below the desk its warmth found the hairline, and the floor began, very quietly, to part. Boof lay down beside the crack to hear it better, chin on the cold slate. Every cricket in the hall stopped at once. So did the pens. Three clerks found themselves looking very hard at a dog. Boof looked back, owl-quiet. She had only lain down. The Genie did not turn from the window. “Lying has two meanings,” he said. “Nobody has ever told the crickets which.” Boof stood. The hum came back as if it had never left. Under the hum, the silence in the room was not peaceful. It was the silence of two wants holding the same breath, kept only because nobody had dared to let it go.

entries.label: Song · The song climbed the…
entries.text: The song climbed the rafters by a narrow stair of notes. One rose for a wish shared out; one held for a wish locked away. Together they made a sound Boof could feel in her teeth, and down in the crack the crickets took the lower note and held it, patient as hens on a cold clutch. She shifted her paw. The crack ran on beneath it, under a pounce-pot and a dropped quill. Whatever the slips said, the floor could not keep both promises.

entries.label: The Fool · The tuning fork hummed…
entries.text: Two receipts on one warmth — the oldest quarrel on the shelf. Somebody wished big here once, and the floor is still paying the note. The tuning fork hummed against the split desk. The wood, not the Fool, was singing — a very old melody, in a key nobody had budgeted for. Dust stood still in the light to listen.

entries.label: Wish-Physics Over the Crack
entries.text: Where the crack left the desk leg for the floor, the clerks had set the crack-gauge: brass calipers as long as a forearm, one jaw on each lip of slate, a small bell at the hinge. It measured in notes, not inches. Every morning the oldest clerk took the note with a fingernail and wrote it in the margin. F at the thaw. F sharp by lambing. When Boof's tail brushed the calipers, the bell gave a note nobody had written yet. The youngest clerk had the wax pot open before the bell had stopped. The oldest put two fingers on her wrist. “Listen before you mend,” he said. It had been the floor's rule since the winter a mason poured lead into the crack without taking its note, and the slate went on singing through the lead all spring, a tone lower and sulking, until they chipped it out. He wrote the new note in the margin first. Then he shut the wax pot himself. The Genie stood astride the crack. “A cart rolling. Rain falling. A Thursday on its way. A wish can turn those.” He nudged a loose edge of slate. “Ask for a little turn, pay a little. Ask the world to swing around you, and somebody else catches the weight.” He bent to the gauge and read it the way he read a price tag. “There's the interest,” he said. “In semitones.” Long ago, someone had wished grandly here. Gold, perhaps. A throne. Nobody remembered the wish. The crack remembered its weight. “Still paying,” he said. Under his slipper, the note went on. The egg did not pick a side. A wish keeps its own law; it is not there to settle other people's wanting. Its heat kept the hairline open and honest, so no one could smooth the seam over with wax and a confident voice and call the quarrel finished. The crickets edged up the crack to sit near it, the way old men edge their chairs toward a stove. Boof left both slips where they hung, pulling at nothing, and turned toward the duskward gate — toward the city that had learned to turn its old breakages into light. A little dried ink clung to the edge of the desk. Boof watched it quiver when the note rose, then rest when it fell. The room had been swept with care. Pens lay straight; the stools were tucked away; whoever worked here had tried to leave things ready for morning. Yet the crack ran beneath all that order, passing under the stool where someone would sit and between the shelves where someone would reach. On the window sill lay a carpenter's door-rule, boxwood and brass, folded shut on a size that matched no door in the hall. Nobody claimed it. It had the look of a thing set down mid-measure. She could follow the crack farther than she could see. Somewhere beyond the wall, a cup began to rattle.

entries.label: Boof · Boof understood the physics…
entries.text: Boof understood the physics better than the hall did, because she had lived it at bowl-height her whole life. A dog who works for the land knows you cannot wish a bowl full; you can only be standing under the bush when the fruit was already going to fall. Redirect, don't create. Her wants had always been small enough to afford. She had simply never known that was a kind of wealth. She had begun, without meaning to, to keep a map. Not the archivist's kind, with roads in it. A map of what kept what: the ants kept the roots warm, the roots kept the berries, the berries kept a little light for whoever came; the grove kept the wants the town would not; the crickets kept the crack's note so it could be heard out. Nothing on it was owned. Everything on it was keeping something else. She did not know yet where the egg went. Her own nose went in the middle, since that was where she read it from. At the archway she looked back once. The door stood ajar on a gold, still room, and from under its floor came the hum, a little higher than it had been that morning. Out in the avenue, the thin song faded into footfall, wheel-rattle, evening trade: a knife-grinder's sparks, a chestnut drum, a coal cart backing into a lane with a great deal of advice. Boof kept the egg close. Ahead, Bonk City's windows caught the last light: old impacts melted into glass, a skyline of things that had been struck and still let someone see through.

entries.label: Boof · Boof trotted into Bonk…
entries.text: Boof trotted into Bonk City the way you step into the acoustic chamber of a struck bell. The streets did not follow straight surveyor lines; they formed a Fool’s Labyrinth of curving bronze posts, rain-slick arches, and leaning panes. The glass of Bonk City was not blown from river sand alone. It was made of old impacts. Anything struck — a dented kettle, a cart's bent rim, a bell cracked one frost-bitten morning — went to the bonk-kiln, which melted the blow out and poured it off clear. So the panes remembered being struck, and had forgiven it into transparency. The kiln stood just inside the gate, breathing a smell like a hot coin. Its soot-furred keeper saw the gold crack in the egg's crown and lifted her tongs. “We take cracks,” she said kindly. Boof stepped wide. This crack was not hers to shut. The lanterns were honest in the one way that mattered — they showed light without claiming to be it. Most were dent-lanterns, and every dent threw a bright crease on the cobbles: a street the light remembers. Some of those streets had since moved. Boof followed one round a bakery and came out where she began, smelling of bread. Every one of them turned its faceted face toward the warm egg in her sling, casting its heat across the cobbles while owning not a single ember of the flame. Then rain came, fine as flour, and the city rang. Its chime-gutters are tuned like a shelf of cups, and a sound roof rings bell-bright. Two lanes along, one rang flat. A roofer stopped mid-bite, said “Cobbler's, back corner,” and went off with the rest of his bun. A lamplighter came down the lane, ringing each post alight with a small brass bell. At every post she shook her lamp-ladder out of its walking-staff shape in three clacks, climbed, rang, and folded it again. “Pie's that way,” she said. “Everything's that way, eventually.” And ahead, down the widest winding street, the smell of boonberries baking rose over the rooftops like a second dusk — because the patron of Bonk City was holding court, and the patron of Bonk City is a pie.

entries.label: Labyrinth · “Every pane will offer…
entries.text: “Every pane will offer you your own warmth,” said a voice behind the glass. Boof turned. Three reflections turned with her. “Very flattering. Very little supper.” In the corner of every pane a glazier had etched two marks: # toward the street, . toward the room. The # face travels, glaziers say; it meets rain and strangers. The . face stays home. This whole alley had been hung backward, and every pane was busy staying, showing Boof herself instead of the way. But pane-snails had been at the soot, grazing it off by night in slow silver loops, and where one had passed the glass was forgiven clear right through: no Boof, no warmth, only a wet step, a cat on a sill, a corner. Boof sniffed a trail, chalk and cold rain, and went the way it showed her. At the corner she lifted her nose. Through the rain and brass came the smell of crust. “There you are,” said the voice. “Glass can show a flame. It can't bake a pie.”

entries.label: The Fool · From the top rung…
entries.text: A lantern is a bruise that learned to give directions. From the top rung of the lamplighter’s lamp-ladder he tapped the brass bell into a crease, and the post remembered heat. Old impact, sampled; returned as light, with interest. That, he remarked to no one and everyone, is the whole city in one honk.

entries.label: The Pie at the Table
entries.text: Every street eventually arrived at a round plaza. At its center, on an oak table, a warm boonberry pie held court. Rain had followed them into the plaza in the folds of coats and the soles of shoes. It steamed from the porters' shoulders while they ate. Before pie, the porters ate boneberries off a brazier at the plaza's rim, a paper cone each, the skins blistered black at the edges. In Bonk City they taste of burnt ends: smoke and crust and a dark sweetness that sticks to the paper. They grow on the kiln walls, where the forgiving heat comes through the brick all winter. Grown, not raised, said the brazier-man, handing Boof the last one in a cone a porter had counted wrong, and he said it the way glaziers say the glass forgives. Boof filed the smell beside the kiln's hot coin, where it belonged. A stall between the chestnut drum and the umbrella-mender sold brace-boxes: small glass boxes with sigil-etched lids, each fogged with a weather nobody had planned. The stall-keeper wrote every lid before she sealed it, so a box could be checked, and refused, before it was made. {frost & hearth} snowed warm flakes on a thumbnail of hearthstone. (cat & bath) held nothing at all. Boof stopped at [grove @ dog], where cedars no taller than barley turned, very slightly, to look at her. Then every box on the shelf brightened toward the egg. “Only what both nouns agree on,” said the stall-keeper, “and they run on borrowed warmth. A week, if nobody holds them.” Boof stepped back and took her warmth with her. The ants at home would not have approved. They knew where warmth came from. Boof settled where she could watch the table legs and the lanes between them, the dropped crumb, the swinging heel, a spoon rescued before it reached the stones. Above her, conversation passed with the plates. Somebody had lost a button; somebody knew a shortcut home; a porter grumbled that the parcel gate's storm-weight groaned on the way up. At the table's end a porter's two children walked brass pie-dividers round a paper pie. It never came out even. There was always a sliver left, thin as a paring, and they argued over it like judges. Between courses their father unrolled something on the table's edge for the younger one to see: a page pressed flat under a sheet of Bonk glass, thin as a leaf and warm from his coat. Under the glass a drawn hill, a drawn dog, a smear where rain had once got in before the glassing and been kept there, forgiven. He turned it over. A second page lay glassed beneath, older, the same hill drawn smaller. Folios, he told the younger one: whenever the story changed you took one to the folio press, which glassed it flat and warm over the last, so nothing known was lost, only layered. Boof put her nose to the edge. It smelled of pressure and heat and, faintly, of the day it was made. The younger one licked a thumb to rub the rain-smear out. “Glass over, never scrape,” said their father before it landed, the glaziers' first law, and the thumb went flat on the glass instead. It left a small print that smelled, to Boof, of boonberry. “Next time this goes under the press, so does that,” said the porter. “Then you're in it.” Across the table a glazier with lead under her nails nodded. “At the map-house they say first ink stays. Same law. Wetter town.” The egg warmed her chest, the ovens warmed her face, and for a little while she could sit among people whose largest unanswered question was whether to have another slice. The knife went in. A slice came out. The pie stayed whole. Boof watched it happen eleven times. A lamplighter ate. A porter took seconds. A child who ought to have been asleep licked the plate. Boof checked beneath the table. No second pie. “People take it for a boast,” said the pie, to the table at large, though nobody had said a word. “Never smaller. It is only arithmetic, and I am very good at arithmetic.” A lamplighter nodded with her mouth full. The pie took this for agreement and beamed at the whole plaza, which is a long way to beam. A server set down another plate and rubbed her wrist. “Enough for everyone,” she told Boof. “Always.” She looked at the washing-up. Boof got off the stool. The server sat. Steam rose from the crust. The pie considered the egg. “If you spent the wish tonight, what would you ask?” Boof opened her mouth. A furrow. A door. The smell of next spring. She could feel the want, but couldn't get its pieces into words. She shut her mouth again. “Good,” said the pie. “Still proofing.” At the far gate, something lattice-crusted shifted in the dark. “Take it out too soon,” he added, more quietly, “and see what you get.”

entries.label: Boof · Boof paused at the…
entries.text: Boof paused at the last curb of the labyrinth and shook the rain from her ears. She carried a slice of BoonWAP wrapped in waxed paper, and the pie behind her was exactly as large as before, and her wish was still wordless and rising somewhere behind her ribs, and all of that was, apparently, correct. She had not eaten the slice. It was warm through the paper, and she was saving it. She could not have said for what. The glass had shown her light without claiming it. The pie had fed a plaza without shrinking. There were ways of being warm in this world that did not require owning the heat. Over the back wall, where no street went, a pair of gate-pigeons rose slowly into the lamplight, fast asleep, hung there a moment, and sank out of sight. She stepped past the last glowing pane into the quiet square. Under the open stars waited an ancient stone slab with a deep circular groove carved into its granite top: the place where oaths are given in public and paid in the honest currency of fruit. The wheel-tracks in the dew ahead of her smelled of hoarded berries. BaneWAP had left the gates before her, and he had come this way.

entries.label: Boof · Boof smelled the market…
entries.text: Boof smelled the market before she saw it: cut cress, wet wool, the chandler's warm tallow, a nettle cheese in dock leaves, last autumn's apples gone wrinkled and crumb-sweet in the dark of a cart. Under all of it lay the sharp blue smell of oaths. Over the bell-arch creaked the market's own weathercock, an iron cousin of the roosters on Council Hill, bought down the slope the year the hill had one opinion too many. The great market stone stood at the center of the square, its granite top worn smooth and dished by centuries of pressing palms. Boof had come to do the one thing the council could not do for her and BaneWAP could not undo: bind herself, in public, to the wish. For an oath here was understood exactly as the Genie had taught her to understand keys — it was a key given away in daylight , handed to the whole watching town at once, so that no one hand could ever secretly grow it. The public half was the words. The private half was paid in fruit, pressed into the rock where centuries of sworn juice had gone before. And the witness was the egg itself, set warm upon the lip of the stone: an unspent wish, watching a promise being made about its own spending. First the fruit was weighed. The oath-clerk had filed keys at the key-file bench on Council Hill until her knees chose the flatter town; her apron was still grey with filings. She took the blueberry Boof had carried in, unbruised in a soft mouth, and set it on the oath-scale, which weighs the fruit an oath is paid in and ignores the hand that pays. A wool-merchant once leaned a ringed thumb on its brass pan for good measure. The needle ignored the thumb, the rings, and the merchant. For Boof's berry it trembled and settled at one: the smallest oath the stone accepts and, the clerk said, the commonest true one. Oaths at the stone are paid in blueberries and nothing else. A boonberry would show the swearer the promise already kept, kindly, a moment early, and who keeps a promise they have already watched come true? A baneberry would say how the promise was going to be broken, and then it would be. A blueberry says nothing at all. Boof, who appreciated blueberries without especially liking them, thought it the best thing she had yet heard said for them. Behind Boof and her one berry, a young drover who smelled of mule waited with a whole basket of last autumn's apples. He had come to swear the whole pass road mended, as long as he lived. The clerk lifted the basket back into his arms. “Promise the next stone, not the road,” she said. “A road is for hoping.” He went red, and thought, and settled on the fallen milestone at the ford: upright by market-day. He kept one apple out to pay with. The rest went to his mule, who had sworn nothing and was delighted. Around the square, stall-holders lifted the weights off their scales, as is done for an oath, so no turnip would be weighed against a promise. Boof pressed the blueberry into the stone. Skin split; juice slipped into the groove worn by other paws and palms. She would spend the wish when the want was true. Not for spite, not for show. Not because a crowd was waiting. The square fell quiet enough to hear a stall-cloth flap. Beneath her other paw, the egg grew warmer. Boof smelled them first: dust and old wool, the inside of a coat pocket. Then the oath-moths came down out of the awning seams, lint-grey. They settle in the groove only when a promise is true. One landed on the juice line. Then three. Then a dozen, wings shut flat as purses, drinking nothing. The whole square watched them instead of the dog. A cheese-wife said moths only liked sugar; the clerk asked why they never sat on her jam. Up on its pin the weathercock turned against the wind to watch — a market weathercock's only vote — and stayed turned.

entries.label: Shadow · But every oath sworn…
entries.text: But every oath sworn in noon light casts one. The shadow lay across the grooves, dog-shaped, egg-shaped, cold, and it was not BaneWAP's — it was the oath's own dark half, the clause nobody reads aloud. The moths sat on in it, unbothered. The Genie read the clause anyway, because pricing things was the one habit he had not liquidated. "Understand what you have promised to spend," he said quietly. "A wish redirects momentum. Redirected momentum lands somewhere. Every spent wish — mine, yours, anyone's — owes one coincidence to a stranger. A cart delayed, a letter misdelivered, a rain moved to a different field. Someone always pays the correction, and they are never at the ceremony." He nodded at the oath-scale. "That weighs what you pay. Nothing in this square weighs what they pay."

entries.label: The Fool · From the dried-fruit stall's…
entries.text: The sworn oath — oldest trope on the shelf. Kings swear on swords. She swore on fruit. Returned with interest. From the dried-fruit stall's crossbeam, among strings of shrivelled berries, he laid it out like a set: the hero's vow, sampled from every saga that ever rattled a mead-hall — swords kissed, blood mingled, thrones promised. He honked it back changed: no blade, no blood, one blueberry, one working dog, and a clause the sagas always skipped — the stranger's bill. That was the interest. An oath that admits its shadow is worth ten that don't.

entries.label: The Shadow Price
entries.text: After the crowd thinned, Boof stayed, chin against the granite. Purple juice dried beside older stains, and the moths kept their places along it like a grey stitch in blue cloth. Somewhere, a stranger would be late because she had wished: a cart missed, a letter lost, rain on the wrong field. She could neither find them nor warn them. The oath gave her no way around that. She sat until the stone cooled beneath her chin. Around her, the square returned to its smaller business. A merchant shook rain from an awning, the cress-seller sluiced her baskets at the trough, a child chased a rolling spool, and two neighbors resumed an argument they had set aside for the ceremony. None of them knew which stranger would catch the turn of her wish. Perhaps that stranger was having an ordinary afternoon too, expecting a letter, counting the hours to supper. Boof watched the spool lodge between two stones. The child knelt to free it. She stayed a little longer, until the crowd had become people again. At the cheese stall a boy wheedled for a wheel cut cheap at the day's end, and was told, as boys in that market are always told, to open nothing before it has filled. She pressed one last blueberry into the central groove until the purple juice welled up and filled the old gold-veined cracks. Payment that smelled true. The lattice-edged shadow at the alley mouth withdrew without a sound — an oath witnessed in public is a poor thing to bid on. The market bell rang the close. The oath-moths lifted all together and went back into the awnings, and the awnings were rolled up with them inside, which they did not seem to mind. Boof lifted the egg back into her sling and turned her nose duskward, toward the ancient well that keeps every face without stealing a single soul.

entries.label: The Fool · His voice thinned with…
entries.text: Swear small, pay in fruit, and tip the stranger you will never meet. His voice thinned with the market bell. Stalls folded into barrows, shadows lengthened, and far away a cart kept someone waiting. No one in the square heard its driver call.

entries.label: Boof · The Watering Eye was…
entries.text: The Watering Eye was a well before it was a witness, and a witness long before anyone built a tavern leaning over it like a drinker over a confession. Boof came in under the sagging floorboards, nose first through spilled lager and wet rope, and set her front paws on the mossy coping. The water below was black and perfectly still, and it did not show her own face first. It showed her an older one — a woman mid-wish, mouth open on a want she had never said aloud — and under that face, folded like pressed linen going down into the dark, every other face the well had ever held. From the barrel-head behind her came the Genie's quoting voice , brisk as a market morning: "I can make you famous by Tuesday, or respected by November. Fame is cheap — reality already leans that way for loud people. Respect requires corrections. Choose." A face said into deep water is not stolen; it is folded, and it stays the property of whoever wore it. The well kept the faces the way good ground keeps rain: patiently, and without letting anyone else spend them. Something down there smelled of a tin cup left in a stream. Then Boof saw them: chalk-pale fish no longer than a spoon, swimming between the faces. Remembrancers, the tavern called them. They went through the faces the way a laundress goes through a basket, tucking a loose chin under, smoothing a brow flat, folding each face gently so it would fit beside the others. One rose to look at Boof and turned politely away, as if she were a face it had not been asked to keep. Overhead the well-winch creaked. The tavern bucket came down past her nose on its wet hemp rope, sank, and was wound up again to the winch song, honey-slow, four beats a turn, so it would not knock anyone on the way. It was a still night. On still nights the bucket comes up holding a face instead of water. The potboy looked in, said "Evening," to whoever it was, and let it back down. The kitchen drew from the rain-butt instead, and the soup tasted faintly of roof.

entries.label: Fold · All night the Genie…
entries.text: All night the Genie dealt in wants. Name one, hear the price, pay or fold. An empire? Quite manageable; the world was forever tipping toward a throne. Supper everyone agreed on? His needle swung so wide it rang against its case; he counted the company twice and quoted three coincidences and a fortnight of Thursdays. At the bar, the regular raised his glass. “Six violations of the natural order,” the Genie told him. “Lager,” said the regular. The Genie wrote it down. After a moment, he underlined it. The locals queued with their wants the way they queued at the winch: a roof mended before the rains, a cousin forgiven, a goat talked back over a wall. They held pewter tankards while they waited and drank them while they thought. A crock of pickled walnuts went round. Every want was smaller than a throne, and every one cost more. A line of torch-ants had come up through a knot-hole at dusk, a long walk from the field, and left a crumb on the barrel-head; the well-damp had put their torch out on the stair. He quoted them nothing, struck a match for their torch-bearer, and wrote nothing down. Old customers. Two beavers, smelling of willow bark and creek mud, took the whole evening over a dam. They wanted the wording exact: the bend, the height, the arrangement of the sticks. By the time they had it right they had drawn it on the table in spilled lager, argued the drawing into a better one, and gone out to build it before the Genie could quote a price. He watched them go with something like professional respect. Beavers, he told Boof, always wished slowly enough to finish the job themselves. Boof had smelled their work all the way up the creek: the water held back in steps, pond over pond, so that it came down to the well slow and clear and never all at once. That was why the Watering Eye had never run dry, and why its faces lay so still. The beavers had never asked the tavern for anything. The tavern left the bark off its firewood on the back step for them, and nobody wrote that down either. Slow work, Boof thought, like the ants: nobody in a hurry, and the whole valley drinking from it. Later the taproom sang: a reel about a miller's daughter, too quick, with clapping, and a carter from over the pass clapped quickest of all. Down the shaft the bucket began to swing. The regular put one hand flat on the bar. Table by table the clapping stopped, the carter's last, and Boof felt it through the boards before anyone heard it: four slow beats a turn, under the reel like a floor under dancers. “The winch song underneath,” said the potboy, winding. “They all are.” The bucket came up even, and knocked nobody.

entries.label: The Fool · He sat the trapdoor's…
entries.text: Eighth honk: the tavern game, sampled and returned — small wants priced dear, because they are the ones the world was not already planning to grant. He sat the trapdoor's edge with his boots over the dark, tapping the game's rhythm on the iron ring, taking the tavern's off-key song — a winch song underneath, like every song in the Watering Eye — and handing it back on-key, with interest.

entries.label: The Unpriceable Want
entries.text: Near closing, he tried Boof again. “Anything. Name it.” She thought of the furrow, the warmth, a trail with something real at its end. His want-needle swung past the numbers and came back blank. He reset it with a thumbnail. She tried again. Same small click, same empty dial. He had the baize case half open to mend the needle when he remembered the clerks at the Rift: listen before you mend. He held it to his ear instead. It ticked as sweetly as the day he bought it. He tried the resolution glass, which cannot see a want smaller than a loaf. It found one at once, in the potboy, who had been eyeing the heel of the last loaf all night. Of Boof it showed only wet stones and an egg. The Genie folded the glass shut with the face of a man whose tools have all, politely, declined. Boof lowered the egg onto the wet stone around the well. Heat spread under her paws, through the coping, down. The folded faces stirred. One by one they turned toward the warmth the way the berries once had. The remembrancers went quick among them, re-folding every face that turned, and for once they fell behind. One rose to the egg's reflection and nosed along it for an edge to fold. It found none. It hung there a moment, pale as a fingernail, then sank back to its work. Then the water said, in the plain way water says things, what every face down there had in common: each one owed a coincidence to a stranger. The egg — an unspent wish — was the debt still standing warm above the fold. The well could not price it either. It only named it, and kept the account open. Boof leaned over the rim without touching the water. Some faces were clear enough to count the lines around a mouth; others drifted beneath reflections of the tavern windows. A laugh came through the floorboards overhead, and for a moment she could not tell whether one of the faces had laughed too. She moved the egg closer. Ripples reached the far wall and came back through the reflected light. The Genie stood beside her with his instruments shut in their baize case. She was glad he had stopped asking her to name it.

entries.label: Boof · "What did I win?"…
entries.text: "What did I win?" Boof wondered, taking the egg back into her sling. The Genie had priced fame, thrones, and six lagers, and had folded on her — the only player at the table whose want his game could not hold. Behind her the regular raised one finger at the dark, on principle. She climbed toward the roofs with the well's answer warming her ribs. Behind her, slow, four beats a turn, the potboy was singing up the last bucket of the night. The egg was a debt. The faces below had turned toward it together, though no voice had called them. Above the ridge, eight old notes hung in the dark. She listened for the missing one and felt it humming against her chest.

entries.label: Boof · The Fool had an…
entries.text: The Fool had an art, and on the ridge above the town he finally showed Boof its bones. He laid his set out on the slates shard by shard — a lineage in nine pieces — for the unit of the art is the honk: a trope sampled from the old tales, sounded in a new mouth, and returned changed, with interest. Each shard hummed the shape of the story it was cut from, and as he set them down in a crescent, Boof could hear where every chamber of their road had come from and where it had been sent back richer. They came out of a shard-rack of smoked ash with nine felt-lined slots. The ninth was egg-shaped, and had been, the Fool said, since long before he knew why; for years he kept a turnip in it so the rack would not look sad. The law of it is short enough for a dog to carry: every trope you sample must be returned changed, with interest. A honk that only repeats is a debt; a honk that returns is a harvest. The slates still smelled of noon's slate-cakes, oat and soot. A few signal-skinks, come up from the flats in a roofer's cart, basked there flicking their tails at the chimney stones, which keep another code. Then, out of the dusk, the geese: nine in a loose wedge, honking in uneven time. Jazz-geese always fly in nines. As each one honked, a shard on the slate rang back. Eight rang. The ninth honk passed over the crescent, found nothing to answer it, and went on into the dark. Boof knew that bent note from the edge of the grove. One goose had taught the Fool his note, or the other way round; neither would say. Eight bells in uneven time is weather, not a set, and Boof's ears had gone flat under it. “One shard at a time,” said the Fool, “or it's only hail.” He lifted the lamp's shard, sounded it against his thumbnail, and set it back in its place before he touched the next. It rang the way the woodcutters say the grove does everything: try it again, a little changed. Then the tree's, then the bottle's, each returned before the next came up. By the fourth Boof could smell where every one had come from: cedar, salt, the iron of a windy hill. The well's came last and slowest, four beats a turn, the winch song underneath, and her paws remembered wet coping. Sounded one by one, they made a road she could follow back.

entries.label: Shard · The Fool laid out…
entries.text: The Fool laid out the shards. Three wishes; a trickster in a tree; a genie lately out of business. A vizier, baked bitter. Two claims splitting a floor. Glass streets, a blueberry oath, a tavern game that couldn't price its quietest player. He touched each piece as he named it, letting the little rings overlap. “Eight.” He slid them together. One space remained. Boof looked at the space, then down at her sling. Then he chalked it on the next slate, as makers do, to check a thing before anyone leans on it: (lamp & tree & bottle & crust & receipt & glass & berry & well & ). Round braces: everything inside must arrive together. Eight pieces of a nine-piece combine are not a smaller combine. They are a heap that hums.

entries.label: The Fool · On the chimney rim…
entries.text: The ninth honk was never sounded. An unspent wish is an unsounded note — and the set was built around its silence. On the chimney rim he breathed through an empty mouthpiece of dark horn. Steam came out, amber. Not sound. Not yet.

entries.label: The Shape with One Hole
entries.text: The egg fitted without a push, and the heap stopped being a heap: eight shards answered together, their separate sounds drawing into one hum. Boof felt it through her nose. Here were the places she had walked, close enough to touch, with a space for what she still carried. The Fool let her look. For once, he had nothing to add, and he chalked nothing into the blank. The slates still held the day's warmth. At the first note the chimney-swifts poured out of the flue in a soot-furred whirl and carried the hum down over the roofs, a little farther than it meant to go. Nothing said on the ridge stays on the ridge; the swifts see to that. Below them, somebody was closing shutters, one clap after another down the street, humming a note she had not had at supper, while a late cart worked its way toward the gate. Boof could have followed any of those sounds to an ordinary evening. Instead she stayed with the pieces. This one caught the light like the grove; that edge brought back the hard feel of the market stone beneath her paw. Some of the places were in sight. Far off, Bonk City's dent-lanterns were coming on, every dent a lane the light remembered. Farther still the salt flats glowed along their whale-roads; where two had wanted one turn, a single line now bent, and a salt-whale was travelling it, slow as weather. And at the very edge of sight, back where she had started, a faint teal glow sat low in the dark like a dropped coin: the miller's pond, holding the light the berry rows let slip, as it did every winter under the ice. She had drunk from that pond every morning of her life and never once thought of it as lit. From up here it was plain that the whole field had been lit from underneath all along: ants to roots, roots to berries, berries to the pond, and the pond to a dog's morning drink. They made a shape together, but she remembered the distance between them, the meals and mud and waiting. No one could have handed her that at the beginning. "A honk is spent breath," the Fool said, lifting the egg free and settling it back in her sling. "A wish is breath still held. Same lineage, opposite ends." The ninth honk would sound when the wish was spent — no sooner, and by the Blueberry Oath, not before the want was true. She left the eight shards singing softly on the rooftop beside the shard-rack, its egg-shaped slot empty again; nobody mentioned the turnip. Then she turned down toward the pass, where the great timber spine of Bone.land waited to be asked what a small thing can hold.

entries.label: Boof · Down the ridge, past…
entries.text: Down the ridge, past roofers' ladders lashed for the night, Boof carried the unsounded note against her ribs. The others could stay on the roof and sing to the chimneys. This one needed walking. She had promised to wait until the want was true; now she knew the silence had been waiting with her. She did not need the eight shards to know her place in the lineage. She had the ninth, folded in its shell against her ribs, and it was leading straight into the massive timber spine of Bone.land, where nothing is trusted until it has proved it can bear weight.

entries.label: Boof · Bone.land did not pretend…
entries.text: Bone.land did not pretend to be theater. Its square-hewn oak beams rose into the morning like the ribcage of a sleeping leviathan, every mortise and peg left exposed to the weather, because this hall was the small constitution — the spine the land trusted to hold when the veil shakes. Boof's nose sorted the place before her eyes did: oak cut that week, quarry chalk, tallow on the hoist ropes. Nothing painted, nothing glued. A peg-boy on a sawhorse was eating a joiner's loaf, rye baked square-cornered so it sits on a beam without rolling off. Beside the loaf the peg-boy had a fistful of boneberries, bone-white with a dusk-red blush, off the tubbed bushes by the anchor stones. The first joiners carried those bushes over the pass, since nothing grows in Bone.land that has not been carried in. He held one down to Boof. It tasted of rib tips: smoke, salt, the good char at the edge, a whole supper in a mouthful, and nobody sorry at the back of it. Grown, not raised, the joiners say, which is as much as they say about it. She trotted across the sawdust floor, and the whole valley heard the frame answer her arrival with one deep BONK — not slapstick, but the sound of a structure declaring itself load-bearing. Sawdust came off the high beams in sheets; the joiners call that sawdust weather. On a scrubbed trestle table between the anchor stones sat something new: a pale, plain pie, steaming faintly, ringed by plumb lines and tuning pegs. Its ingredients were pricked into the rim of its crust. Boof checked the list with her nose. It was complete. "Mx. BoneWAP," it said, by way of everything. "Load-bearing. I listen to what things will carry. Set the wish on the frame, please." Where BaneWAP was hoarded berries gone bitter in a banker's crust, and BoonWAP served himself and was never smaller, BoneWAP was clean-boiled honesty: no sugar it had not declared, no filling it could not show. In Bone.land, even a pie keeps its joints exposed. Boof made for the nearest beam. "Not that one," said BoneWAP. "Read the mortise marks." Beside every joint a joiner had cut a caret ^ where the beam lifts, a dot . where it stands. That beam was a lifter, and you do not ask a lifting thing a question; it is busy. Frames here are chalked on the floor in braces and marks before anyone raises them, because chalk is cheaper than oak and a mistake in braces falls on nobody. The marks are what is left of the argument. Boof found a dot on the sill beam and set the sling down there. Boof's nose found fresh chalk before her eyes found the joiner, on her knees across the hall, drawing tomorrow's frame on the boards. The peg-boy asked, through loaf, why she didn't just cut it. She sat back, found two braces meeting wrong, scuffed them out with her heel and drew them again a hand's width over. “Chalk is cheaper than oak,” she said. Every joiner says it. The bench by the door is why: cut from the one beam in living memory raised before it was chalked. It is very comfortable. Nobody likes sitting on it.

entries.label: Bonk · The egg went onto…
entries.text: The egg went onto the frame. A weight slid, a beam settled, and the little brass load-bells under the joists rang one after another down the brace until the weight reached the anchor stone and went quiet in the chalk. Boof could hear exactly where the egg was being carried. BoneWAP lifted the listening mallet, felt-headed and worn pale at the grip, and tapped the sill beam once. Not a blow; a question. A beam struck hard tells you only that it has been struck. A low note ran through the frame into Boof's paws. In the cracks of the timber the load-beetles listened. They click when a beam is asked to bear more than it agreed to, and every beam here is told its load out loud on raising day, the way a child is told its chores. Not one clicked. The answer came up through the wood in gold: the smallest wishes have the longest arcs. Given the current, a small turn could travel generations.
