Then BoneWAP tapped again and asked the other question — what if the whole river were forced round a throne? The load-beetles went off along the tie-beam like rain starting on a roof, ridge to sill. The corrections would come downstream, roof by roof. Boof shook the ringing from her ears. It stayed in the wood.

entries.label: The Fool · He hung from the…
entries.text: Plaster sneezes. Oak does not. Grand wishes are plaster; small ones are the spine. He hung from the collar-beam like a bright bat and knocked. The oak answered as law, and the pie below him signed it.

entries.label: What the Frame Would Bear
entries.text: BoneWAP did not whisper the answer to a council or fold it into a drawer. It let the hall ring — and a hall that size, struck true, is heard in every kitchen of the valley. The chimney-swifts carried it farther than it meant to go, flue to flue, until kettle-lids hummed it on hearths that had never heard of Bone.land. By noon the note had gone out on the pass road, to the tavern, to the Watering Eye, where people said it back to one another. Down in the well the remembrancers rose through the folded faces to listen, and the well-winch turned a quarter-turn by itself, as if the bucket wanted to hear too. The Egg’s wish, spent small and true, would cost one lent coincidence and a spare Thursday, and its arc would outlast every roof in the valley. The grand wish a certain bitter pie intended would call in a generation of coincidences — a whole town’s luck, drawn without asking. Boof had heard it once before, for nothing, from a genie in the sand: build where the land already leans. People stopped to hear it with baskets on their arms and tools still in their hands; a cooper forgot to set down his half-hooped barrel. Some hummed the note to check it; some asked a neighbor to say it again. It traveled out of the hall in voices that sounded nothing alike. At the anchor stones two carters began to argue the sum, louder each time round. A joiner handed them a stub of chalk without a word. Write it before you argue it, they say on Council Hill; Bone.land adds only that you do it on the floor. They wrote it. Halfway across the boards they found they agreed, and were annoyed about it, and finished anyway. A clerk from the hall of arches had carried the crack-gauge up the pass to compare floors. Set across the tie-beam, the brass calipers closed to a hair and hummed the note back higher and cleaner than the Rift's: the same law, a younger floor, nothing owed yet. Boof heard one person stumble over the sum and another get impatient, then go back and help. By afternoon the saying had softened at its edges, the way told things do. A child kept the note going while an older neighbor finished the sentence. There was no bell to mark the moment the news became theirs. The note was still in the beams when word came up the pass: the bitter pie had heard it. He had understood it. He had stopped waiting. Boof felt the tremor before she heard the messenger's feet. Above her, the pegs held; dust drifted from a beam; somewhere in the tie-beam a single load-beetle clicked at a weight nobody had set down yet. She checked the sling.

entries.label: Boof · "Is this where the…
entries.text: "Is this where the trail terminates?" Boof asked the king-post. The Fool answered with a soft knock on the honest oak — no. A true test does not end a story; it only takes away the story's excuses. Everyone in the valley now knew what the wish cost small and what it cost grand, and one bitter pie had decided the arithmetic applied to other people. Nothing grew in Bone.land that had not been carried in. In her sling, beside the egg, the slice from Bonk City was still warm through its waxed paper. She had carried it over the pass without eating it. She did not know why, and she did not take it out. She settled the egg deeper against her chest and turned downhill, toward the road the bitter smell was climbing. Behind her, the timber answered the shaking with small creaks, peg to socket, joint to joist. Ahead, the road looked much as it had that morning. She went carefully.

entries.label: Boof · Below Bone.land the road…
entries.text: Below Bone.land the road ran through an old bloom garden nobody had kept for years. Quince had gone to riot over the walls, the blackthorn hedge stood white with flower, and a moss-thick sundial pointed at the wrong hour without minding. Boof smelled sap, sloe-blossom, a straw bee-skep warming in the sun. Then cold pastry. It happened between one honest sniff and the next. Where the frame's note still hung in the air, Mr. BaneWAP stopped shadowing and simply took — banker's crust cracking with the effort, tin lockbox open and shut, the egg gone from Boof's sling before her growl could finish forming. He did not run far. He did not need to. “Behold!” he announced to the bloom garden, which had not asked. “A wish the size of an empire, spent all at once, and not one clause about giving it back.” There was a clause. There is always a clause. He had written it himself, at the bottom, very small, and he never read the bottom of anything. All around the rise, on the shut quince buds, the early bees were already waiting. They come a week before the blossom and hum at closed petals as if the bloom owed them. Boof had always thought it a poor way to spend a spring. He had been saying it for a week, to anyone who would stand still: an empire, whole, at once. That is how a baneberry foretells, and he was made of them. Say a thing that will go wrong often enough, and loudly enough, and the world begins arranging itself to have heard you. Boof had smelled it on the wheel-tracks all the way down from the pass: not the crust, the saying, cold and plum-dark and sure of itself. Nobody had stepped on it in time. He stood on a low rise with the warm shell in both crimped hands and wished the wish he had been drafting since the auction failed: an empire, whole, at once. And the wish — this is the part no one had priced — granted instantly. It was a moment of bloom before seed . Every bud in the garden opened at once, for him, with a sound like a drawer pulled out. The early bees went in and came straight out again. A flower opened on demand has not had time to fill. Over the wall came the beekeeper whose skeps stood along its foot, her veil half on. Her bees were walking the open petals and coming away with nothing. She looked at the flowers, and at the pie on the rise, and said to nobody who would listen, “Open nothing before it has filled.” Then she went down the row stopping each skep door with a twist of grass, so her bees would stay home until there was something to fetch. It has been the beekeepers’ rule ever since. Karmic momentum does not refuse a grand wish. It simply pays it out the way momentum pays everything: one coincidence at a time, minimum-viable, corrections deferred. A barn deed blew against his crust. A road bent to end at his feet. A distant clerk misfiled a fortune in his name. The empire arrived. It arrived mediocre. It arrived in pieces. The throne came first, shed at the garden gate by a players' wagon that hit a rut at the convenient moment — a stage prop, gilt over pine. The throne smelled rented: hire-straw and other people's sitting. Banners came after, lifted off a dyer's line by an obliging gust, in colors nobody had ordered. Subjects arrived halfway through errands. One still held a loaf. Boof watched the new emperor wait for the scene to feel complete. It kept arriving. It never did. The crown came last, as crowns do. The wish did not make one; it found one. All spring the crown-wasps had been building in the blackthorn — grey paper chewed from fence rails and old auction notices, ribbed and turreted and very fine — and the nearest of their crowns came loose and settled on his crust. It was beautiful. It was hollow. It was still occupied. Boof heard it before he did: a dry, papery hum, a rented thing with tenants. Every rented crown is wasp-work, if you hold it to your ear.

entries.label: Bloom · Deep beneath his crust…
entries.text: Deep beneath his crust, a berry woke. The wish had passed through him, leaving its drop of light just as it had in the fields. One seam shone, then another. Warmth worked through the bitter filling. He tasted what he had kept from everyone, himself included. Sweet. It had been sweet all along. Around him, the banners stirred. He made a small sound the throne did nothing to support. “It was only ever rented,” he said, to nobody. Then, because a foiled pie always says one thing more than it means to: “The crown was wasps.” Wasps know sweetness before anyone. The crown-wasps came down out of their paper crown in a slow grey trickle, walked the flaking crust where the sweet was pushing through, and drifted off toward the quince. The crown stayed on his head, empty now. It weighed exactly what it was.

entries.label: The Fool · He tapped the rented…
entries.text: The Midas touch, sampled: everything he grasped turned to more, and none of it to enough. Sound it, send it back sweeter. That is the whole law. He tapped the rented throne once — hollow, gilt over pine — and let the note say what the timber had: interest is owed on every borrowed want.

entries.label: The Wish That Would Not Finish
entries.text: Here is the paradox the timber had circled without naming: a wish only leaves its shell when it is finished, and a wish the size of an empire is never finishable. There is always one more coincidence owed, one more correction pending in some far county where a stranger's luck must be bent to balance a king's. The grant kept arriving and kept not being done. The empire stood, hollow as a rented crown, and the egg in BaneWAP's hands stayed exactly as warm as it had been in the frozen furrow — spent and unspent at once, a note held but not released. The banners had shaken the hedges, and rehearsal moths blundered out into daylight like guests at the wrong hour, a long way from the grove. Their wings carry tomorrow's weather, a little smudged. Today they carried the empire's: rain coming on over a court with no roof, arriving in instalments. At the edge of the new court, a woman still holding her market basket asked whether she could go home. A banner brushed her shoulder. A rehearsal moth sat on the basket handle, opening and closing the rain. No one answered; the emperor was staring at his own hands. Boof could smell bread cooling in the basket, a seed-loaf still warm on its underside, and dust rising where the throne had scraped the ground. The empire needed this woman to be a subject. She needed to get the bread indoors before rain; she had read the moth. Boof watched her take one step backward, then another. The banner lifted, and she slipped beneath it. His crimped hands softened. The egg slipped, tipped, rolled down the rise, past a banner dragging in the dust, through quince petals that had opened too soon. Boof stepped forward. It came to rest against her paws, warm as ever. The crack had widened enough to show gold within. She checked the shell with her nose: hot iron, sap, a little sweetened crust. Still humming. Still waiting. She left the crack alone. She had watched a whole garden opened early that morning. That night, wherever she set the sling down, the ground beneath it was busy by morning: torch-lines bent toward the shell from every root within reach, and the frost drew back a hand's width, as if something under the loam had been given more to work with. Whatever was in the egg, it was not keeping its warmth to itself. An early bee was waiting on the sling's knot, as if the egg owed it something too. Boof let it wait.

entries.label: The Fool · He pointed downhill, past…
entries.text: Eight honks sounded. The ninth still sleeps in the shell. Small wishes travel farthest. He pointed downhill, past the last of the blackthorn, to two rivers that had not yet agreed to forget their springs, and Boof — who finally almost knew her want — went to meet them.

entries.label: Boof · The confluence smelled of…
entries.text: The confluence smelled of two springs at once: one water chalk-pale and quarry-cold, the other berry-dark and sweet with far orchards. River tar on the planks. Under it all, warm shell. Two great mountain rivers met beneath a wide, low-planked timber bridge, and it was there, muzzle over the rail with the egg warm between her paws, that Boof finally knew. Not a hunch. Not the shape of a want seen sideways. She knew, the way a true scent is known at its end, and the wish was small enough to hold in a mouth: that the land keep one warm furrow open — always — for whatever arrives next without a receipt. Below her the waters ran in an unblended seam — berry-dark and chalk-pale sharing one bed without forgetting their springs — and she understood that her wish was the same shape as the river: a membrane, not a merger. Room made, nothing owned. A seam-otter came down the channel exactly on the line, one paw in each water, rolling without ever choosing a side. Its fur dried berry-dark on one flank and chalk-pale on the other; boatmen swear there are two kinds of otter here. There is one kind, wet in both waters. The Off-Season Genie had followed her since the third chamber, because her wants were too small for instruments built for emperors. He heard it and went very still — the way a craftsman goes still when the one job his tools were never sized for turns out to be the job he stayed retired for. He laid his instruments on the rail one last time. The want-needle did not circle; it found Boof and held, like a dog on a point. The wish-scale would not settle at a coincidence, or a season of them, or a lifetime; it kept tipping, honey-slow, toward always. “Build where the land already leans,” he murmured: his oldest advice, and the only thing he had ever priced at nothing. The ants had kept that field warm every winter Boof could remember. She was only asking it to go on. The Genie counted the price onto the rail. Once, he'd said a small wish cost a coincidence and a Thursday. This one asked for always. He emptied what remained in his reserve and kept his hand open beside it. “Everything left,” he said. “Plus one Thursday.” Boof looked from his hand to his face. Neither bargained. Last he opened the bottle-desk's narrow drawer for Thursdays. Empty: he had spent them all on emperors. This one would come out of the week ahead. He folded the desk shut for good, with a small brass click like a shop door at closing, and left it on the rail.

entries.label: Path · Far upcountry, frost loosened…
entries.text: Far upcountry, frost loosened along one furrow. The ground warmed and stayed warm. That night the torch-ants moved beneath it. With less heat to make, they could tend more roots; their torch-lines ran farther along the furrow than they had in years, and a beetle who had been cold since autumn — a load-beetle, a long way from any timber — found a lit street. The berry rows widened through the winter. The ants had known the Genie longer than anyone, and they were the only ones who noticed what always had cost him. A stranger would receive a good coincidence. Somewhere in the coming week, a Thursday quietly went missing. On the bridge, no thunder. Only water under wood, and the Genie putting his empty hand away. Downstream an ink-heron lifted out of the berry-dark shallows for the first time that season. It had stood so still that its reflection had dried into the bank, and it left the reflection behind on the mud.

entries.label: The Fool · Spent to the last…
entries.text: The last-wish trope, sampled: the genie spends the final granting on himself — and he does not fade. He posts himself to the grove and accrues. Spent to the last coin of himself, the Off-Season Genie walked upstream into the grove that keeps echoes, and became its next one — a granting you can visit. By the week's end the echo-wrens in the hollow cedars had a new call, a beat late: a small dry cough, like a man clearing his throat before a price.

entries.label: Both Receipts Posted
entries.text: Then the last threads came down the road to the bridge, because a confluence gathers. Mr. BaneWAP arrived first, walking soft, his banker's crust gone flaky and generous where the awakened berries had re-sweetened him from the inside out. It came away in grey curls as he walked, thin as crown-wasp paper. At the landing he stopped and rang the ferry-bell, which is rung by anyone who needs to cross the seam without wetting both springs, or who doubts the bridge will hold them. The ferryman pointed his pipe at the planks. BaneWAP stepped on. The load-bells beneath the deck rang under him once each, small and light, all the way out to where Boof stood. He had been heavier the last time anything weighed him. He had no coin fit for the apology he owed, so he paid in the only currency a pie has: he split himself, clean down the crimp, and offered the slices to the road. And Mr. BoonWAP — who serves himself in slices and is never smaller — received him warm, the way Bonk City receives everything, and showed him the trick of it: giving is not subtraction if the filling is true. “I have always said so,” said BoonWAP, who had never once said so, to the ferryman, who had not asked. Mr. BaneWAP opened his mouth to announce something dreadful, from habit, and found he had nothing dreadful left. He announced instead that he would be very bitter about all of this, starting tomorrow, unless somebody was kind to him first. BoonWAP was, at once, at length, and without noticing that it had worked. It was the first thing he had ever foretold that came true the kind way. Boof smelled it go by: plum-dark at the bottom still, and sweet all the way up. Mx. BoneWAP arrived last, clean-boiled and exact, with the oath-scale from the market stone under one arm. It weighed both slices and found them equal; the oath-scale ignores the hand that pays. BaneWAP drew breath to swear he would never be bitter again. “Promise the next stone, not the road,” said BoneWAP, who had it from the oath-clerk, and he swore to the slice instead. Most days the rail-pins held the bridge's small news: ferry hours, a lost goat, a recipe for eel pie the pies present politely did not read. BoneWAP posted both receipts among them for any traveler to read: one slice given in apology, one slice received in welcome, sources named, nothing flattened. Grey oath-moths came in off the market road and settled on the receipts, one to each; they settle only where a sworn word is true. And here was the quiet miracle of the small wish already at work — both receipts could hang side by side, because the wish had aligned them. The whole confluence held: berry water and chalk water, bitter pie and boon pie, hall and grove, all sharing one bed along a living seam, a membrane that shares without giving the house away. It was the council's law from the hill, &[boon, bane]{table}, written this time in water instead of pine. The boatmen have a plainer name for it. “Two springs, one bed,” said the ferryman, and went back down to his boat, which carries two bailing-cans, one stained berry-dark and one chalk-white. He has never once bailed one water with the other’s can. In forty years the boat has never once gone down. The egg in Boof's sling was lighter now, and its heartbeat had changed from waiting to arriving. Boof listened to the travelers crossing behind her, the different weights of their steps — a drover, two goats — and the pause where someone stopped to look down. Under the bridge, one river carried a darker thread for a while before the currents loosened it. She followed the color as far as she could. Upstream lay the places each had come from, still there even after she could no longer tell the waters apart. The egg rested easily in its sling. For the first time in days, she shifted her shoulder without arranging it around a weight.

entries.label: Boof · "Where does a spent…
entries.text: "Where does a spent wish go?" Boof asked the twilight, nose lifted toward the archive downstream. Nowhere, said the warm wind off the far furrow. It stays. It becomes a place you can stand. Below the path the moon came up and laid a lane of light along the seam. At the landing the ferryman chalked it on his slate, as ferrymen do every clear dusk — <river ~ moon> — not to make the moonrun, which the river makes itself, but so no stranger mistakes it for a place to stop. You can go through. Nobody stays. Boof followed the gravel path downstream. The egg rode lightly now, its song rising through sack and strap. Eight notes behind her, one gathering under her chin. Beyond the bend stood the archive. She could hear the river through its open door.

entries.label: Boof · The round room at…
entries.text: The round room at the end of the river path was smaller and quieter than any map had promised. The seam-otters that had swum beside Boof down the bank turned back at its steps, where the rivers blended and left them no seam to swim. Over the steps, the lintel remembered the springs anyway. Someone had cut the boatmen’s name for the rivers into it: two springs, one bed. It was here, on the polished slate at the center of the rotunda, that the finished wish did the one last thing a finished wish is required to do. It sounded. The ninth honk — the one the Fool had carried unsounded through eight chambers of sampled tropes, the shard that had slept in the shell since before the frost — left the egg as one clean note and rolled out over the whole land at once. Over the dawnward field and its one kept furrow, over the grove with its newest echo, over Bonk City serving itself in slices, over Bone.land's honest joists, over two rivers sharing a bed without forgetting their springs, where the ferry-bell shivered on its post with no hand on the rope. Boof stood in the middle of it with her ears full of gold and understood that she was hearing a return path made of sound: every trope the set had sampled, coming home changed, with interest. And when the note settled, the maps — the same maps that had beaded and refused since the first morning — finally took the ink. The first line they accepted, before any border or crown, was the warm furrow. Nobody wrote it. The land set it down itself, line by line, having at last agreed to know what had happened to it. On the drying-line along the back wall, every map that had ever refused a line stopped dripping into the trough. Boof went round the room by nose. Cedar, beeswax, iron-gall ink. Oak roof-beams cut with mortise marks, ^ where they lifted, . where they stood. Slate laid whole, without a crack, and so without hum-crickets. The quiet was its own. The archive kept a little of everything the land had met. Rehearsal moths in a jar, their wings smudged with tomorrow's frost, then a blur where a day should be. Brace-boxes gone cold in a drawer; an archive keeps the recipe, not the warmth. On the high window, far from Bonk City, a pane-snail grazing a clean lane for the starlight. One drawer had no label but a pencilled line, a box for what you do not know, and it stood a little open. Each ring of shelves ended in a gap, and in each gap sat a shelf-owl, grey as a page-edge, round as a loaf. When Boof put her nose into the nearest gap, the owl opened one lamp-oil eye and clacked its beak, the way a librarian clears her throat. The gap smelled of feathers and nothing else. The owls kept it clear for chronicles not yet written; they nested in what was missing, and would not have a nose in it. Boof took her nose back. She knew a kept place when she smelled one. Over each ring of shelves a rule was cut into the cedar, in letters a hand high. Over the maps: first ink stays — and the first ink on them now was the furrow. Over the mending bench, where torn pages waited to be heard out: listen before you mend. Over the songbooks, each with the same four beats pencilled under its tunes: the winch song underneath. Boof read them the way she read most things, by nose. The oldest cuts smelled of hands. Beside the great book stood a bowl of cold spring water. Boof drank. The dust of the journey washed from her throat. On the nearest shelf lay two copies of a map, held open by press-stones: three corners weighted, the fourth curled. One press-stone is always missing, even here. In one, a white thread of path ran between a garden wall and the river. In the smaller copy, the lines touched. Someone had penciled in the margin: leave room for the path. Lower down, in the same pencil, a small unshaded fox trotted off the edge of the page. Under it: page-fox. Boof sniffed the first page. Wet grass. She sniffed the second. Only paper. Boof lifted her head and looked back the way she had come. Every ring of shelves broke where the aisle ran through it, door to desk, and each ring was packed so tight a whisker would not have gone between its books, right up to the owl and the gap at its end. Whoever built the place had left room for the path first, and fitted everything else round it.

entries.label: Record · The great book lay…
entries.text: The great book lay open on a cloth from the crosswind loom, whose weave still shifted color in the draught from the door. No one stood over it. An oath. An apology. A genie's whole reserve, and one Thursday besides. The pages held what each had cost, each filed as a small realm in braces — {oath}, {apology}, {reserve & Thursday} — a room a reader could stand in for a minute. A brace that closed was a finished record. One that would not close was still happening. Boof had carried a want until she knew its shape. Now the wish was spent and the note had sounded. On the desk sat the shell. Empty. Light. She nosed its rim. Still warm.

entries.label: The Fool · The Boonberry Fool bowed…
entries.text: Thirteen chambers, nine honks, and every borrowed trope gone home changed — warmer than it left. The Boonberry Fool bowed, and for once said nothing clever. He set each borrowed thing back where it belonged: the found egg, warmer; the greedy wish, sweeter; the echo, somewhere you can visit; the small wish, a furrow that never closes; and the happily-ever-after, changed — an ever-after that leaves its last line blank. He set his tokens on the shelves as he named them — a bell, a mask, a bone die, a berry — never in a gap. Last, on the bottom shelf, his shard-rack: eight dull shards, and the egg-shaped ninth slot empty. He had learned the set one shard at a time, and he did not hurry the slot that was left.

entries.label: The Blank Last Line
entries.text: Boof looked from the book to the open shell-shaped door. The first map had refused her egg. This one held the road she had walked, all the way back to the warm furrow. She followed it with her nose. Grove, gate, river bend. Here was a place she had been afraid. Here, a place she had eaten. It was not her map. Hers had no roads in it, only what kept what: the ants keeping the roots, the roots keeping the berries, the berries keeping their light for the pond, the beavers keeping the water slow, the kilns keeping every blow and forgiving it. Baneberries in the hedge-bottoms, saying things; boonberries under the ice, seeing kindly; boneberries feeding whoever came and promising nothing. The book had drawn where she went. She had drawn, without a pen, why any of it was still there. Where the egg went on it she still could not have said; only that everywhere it had been was a little warmer. At the end, one line stayed blank. Every other page in the book had been glassed in the glassing press behind the desk, an upright thing of oak and iron with a screw as thick as a mill-shaft: pressed clear and kept, season over season, the older lines still legible under the new. A folio press does a page at a time; the glassing press did the land. It had pressed every page but this one. That was why it could still take a line. Its crossbeam bore the glaziers’ law: glass over, never scrape. The line began with a brace: an open brace, and no close. A room with one wall unbuilt, which nobody could stand in yet and anybody might walk into. The Fool waited. The pen waited. Nothing came. At last he set the empty shell beside the line, ready for the next wish. The great press ticked as it cooled. The shelves had room; the shelf-owls saw to that. The door stayed open.

entries.label: Boof · Boof rested her chin…
entries.text: Boof rested her chin beside the shell. Its warmth reached through the wood. Outside, a cart rattled past. A bell rang once. She lifted an ear. Nearby, this time. It stayed nearby. Morning spread across the farms. Smoke rose from kitchens; someone would soon be cutting bread. Far off, one furrow steamed in the frost. Boof turned toward the door. An early bee had got there first and hung humming in the shell-shaped arch, as if the morning were a bloom that owed it an opening. Boof lingered with her nose just beyond the arch, where the cool air met the room's last warmth. The road smelled of damp gravel, horse, a little spilled grain. Behind those came the less certain scents of places she had not visited. Nobody called her back to explain the ending. Inside, the Fool moved a chair away from the desk so there would be room to approach it. Boof heard the legs scrape, then settle. She waited until the cart had passed before stepping into the road. Where its dust settled, a hat hung in the air at the height of a person's head — round-crowned, brimmed, touching nothing. It was a little farther down the road each time she looked. She could not smell who was under it. She could smell that someone was. Behind her, the shell kept warm. The last line waited.

entries.label: The Wrong Quiet
entries.text: Dawn smelled of frost and wet fur, and of nothing else at all. Boof put her nose to the ground and read the field the way she read it every morning. Frost on the furrows. Loam under the frost. The berry rows asleep beneath their ice, each holding its drop of light, and down among the roots the torch-ants at their hearths, keeping the winter honest. Everything was where it belonged. Nothing was happening to any of it. The latch did not lift at the kitchen. The bucket did not knock the well. No smoke stood up from the chimney, and yesterday's bread smell had gone thin and stayed thin, the way a smell does when nobody is coming to cut the loaf. She put her nose to the crack beneath the kitchen door. Cold stone. Old onions. Nobody. At the mill the water ran under the wheel and the wheel did not turn. The miller's boot-scraper still wore a ridge of last night's mud along its blade. Boof sat beside it for as long as the miller usually took to come out and swear at the weather. The weather went unsworn at.

entries.label: Boof · Boof did not keep…
entries.text: Boof did not keep a week. She kept mornings. Each one came with its own smell and she took it as it came. A person has to be told what day it is. A dog only has to be there. Keep the morning, not the week, the shepherds say of a good dog, and it is the highest praise they have. So she did not know it was Thursday. She did not know that, not long before, on a bridge where two rivers met, a retired genie had counted everything he had left onto the rail and added one Thursday besides — or that the week had closed over the gap like water over a dropped stone, so that every person in Boon.land had gone to sleep on Wednesday and would wake on Friday without the faintest sense of having missed a thing. She knew only what her nose told her. The people were not in this day. Everything else was. The blackbird was on the fence, trying the same few notes until one pleased it. The crows were in the stubble. The river was at its slow work and the frost at its quick one, and under the berry rows the ants carried their small lights home along the roots. And some things were in the day that were in no other. In the lane, between the frost-ruts, a little herd of hob-deer was grazing — deer no taller than a boot, dun-backed and white at the tail, cropping rime off the verge with small exact teeth. They smelled of dry bracken and cold pennies. They did not run from her. Hob-deer walk only on days nobody keeps, and nobody had ever been out in one to teach them to run. Whatever had taken the day out of the week had taken it only from those who kept one. Nobody had been able to take it out of the field. Boof considered this for about as long as it takes to scratch behind one ear. Then she went to walk the fences. If the people had been taken out of the day, the fences had not, and they would want checking either way.

entries.label: Boonberry · The berries noticed first…
entries.text: The berries noticed first. They always did; noticing is most of what a boonberry is for. Every morning since the wish, the little lights under the ice had leaned toward the warm furrow, the way a sleeper turns to the warm side of the bed. This morning they leaned, and then each one corrected — a quarter turn, all the way down the rows, with a small sound like frost settling. Not toward the furrow. Square to it. As if something were standing there that could only be looked at from the side.

entries.label: The Hat Above the Furrow
entries.text: The warm furrow was steaming when she reached it. It always steamed now. That was the wish: one furrow kept open, always, for whatever arrived next — an open brace in the field, with no close. The frost drew back from it in a soft margin of hearth-drift, rime and steam taking turns at the edge, and beneath it the ants worked late into the coldest nights, and a beetle or two had moved in for the winter and been made to feel at home. This morning the ant-streets were wrong. Ant-streets follow roots, and roots follow water, curling and doubling back, so the little lights had always run in curls. Now, for an arm's length on either side of the furrow, they ran straight. They met at right angles. One line of torches climbed the furrow's wall to the lip of the frost and stopped there as neatly as if someone had ruled it and lifted the pencil. Above that place, at the height of a person's head, the hat was waiting. It was the hat from the road. Round in the crown, short in the brim, black as a stove. It rested on nothing. Steam rose into the gap beneath it, parted around the gap the way water parts around a stone, and closed again above. Boof circled the furrow once, slowly. No tracks in the frost. No scent but steam and ant-smoke and her own breath. She circled it again. She did not dig. Open nothing before it has filled, the beekeeper had said in the bloom garden, and Boof had seen that garden opened early. The second time round, the steam had a shape in it. A circle, under the hat. Below the circle, a rectangle. Two lines down from the rectangle and two lines out from its sides. It was not a person made of steam. It was a drawing of a person, done the plainest way there is, by someone who had not had much time and had not wanted to waste any. Where the steam thinned, the lines stayed. He was not facing her. He was not facing the house, or the road, or the grove. He was facing exactly a quarter turn away from all of it, toward a place on the furrow's edge where nothing seemed to be. Boof could not smell him. She could smell that someone was.

entries.label: Boof · She went to see…
entries.text: She went to see what he was looking at, because that is what a dog does with somebody else's attention. It was an ant. One ant, at the very end of the ruled street, holding up a torch that had gone out — a splinter of root-pith no longer than a barley-awn, black at the tip. It held it the way you hold up a thing to show that it is broken, before you are ready to say it can't be mended. Two dots had arrived in the circle of his head while Boof was looking at the ant. She had the strong impression that they had not been there before, and that they would not always be. Then he did a thing Boof had no word for. He lifted one arm — a line — and lowered the end of it to the ant's torch, and the end of the line was lit, a little, as if it had always been a wick and had only now been asked. The torch caught. The ant inspected it. It turned it this way and that, in the manner of someone who has been sold a bad torch before, and decided this one would do. It went home down the straight street without looking back. He lowered the arm. It was shorter than the other one now. Not by much — by about the length of an ant's torch. Boof looked at that arm, and at the other arm, and at that arm again. Nobody explained.

entries.label: Path · When he moved, he…
entries.text: When he moved, he did not walk. He was in one place, and then in the next place along, as if the day were being told in pictures and somebody had skipped the ones in between. Then a pause. Then the next picture. Boof had followed hares, and hares did not do that. She had followed the Genie's directions, and even those did not do that. He went straight. The lane out of the field bends twice, once around the miller's pond and once around the old stone with the iron ring in it, and he did not bend with it. He crossed the frozen pond on the shortest line. He passed the stone without minding it. Where the hedge stood in his way he went through, and afterward there was a gap in the hedge: a neat rectangle exactly his size, its cut edges green, as if the hedge had always grown that way and was only now admitting it. A moment later a fox came through the new gap at a quick trot, the color of an unturned page, head low, as if late for something it had been told about in another week. It did not look at either of them. Boof had no word for it. The archive downriver had one, penciled in a margin: page-fox. Higher in that same margin, in the same pencil: leave room for the path. The hedge seemed to have taken it to heart. Boof took the lane. She had paws, and they were not the kind for crossing ponds. It did not matter. Wherever the lane straightened, he was ahead on it. Direction was enough to follow. The scenery could do as it liked. The scenery did as it always did, and with nobody in it Boof could see it plainly. The miller's pond was lit faintly teal from under the ice, where the light the berry rows let slip comes to rest all winter; two mill ducks stood on the warm patch with their feet tucked up, arguing. Up the creek the beavers' steps held the water slow. Under every root she passed, a torch went by. Nobody was keeping any of it. All of it was being kept. The lane went round the old stone with the iron ring, and so did Boof. Words had been cut into its weathered side long ago, at the height a hand comes to rest when a walker stops for breath: promise the next stone, not the road. She did not need to read them. She could smell how many hands had rested there on the way past, and that told her most of what they said. Frill-lichen had grown round the cut letters, as it does on any stone that has been read aloud: a grey-green ruffle with more edge than room, crowding every margin, folding and folding, and never once running out of edge. She stopped once, at the house, for something from the shelf by the cold stove: a slice of BoonWAP in waxed paper that she had carried out of Bonk City a long way back and never eaten. It was still warm. It had no business being warm. She did not know what she was saving it for. A long walk was reason enough to bring it. All that Thursday they crossed the land in their two ways, his straight and hers bent. Past the grove that keeps echoes, where the echo-wrens sang from the hollow cedars a beat late and the grove repeated the hat a beat late too, and then could not decide where to put it — and something in there that sounded a little like an old genie said, to nobody, “Ah. There it is.” The woodcutters say the grove only ever does one thing: try it again, a little changed. It tried the hat again, a little higher, and again, until it hung at a person’s height above nothing, which seemed to satisfy it. At the grove's edge, hoofprints pressed into the frosted moss beside Boof's own, a beat after she had made hers. Nobody had ever seen the lag-stag. Nobody saw it now. But it had never before walked beside anyone. Along the river path, where the ink-herons stand so still that their reflections dry into the bank. Where he passed, the dried herons on the mud came out plainer than the birds above them: a few clean lines apiece. Up the long rise toward the Bonk City road. A skein of jazz-geese came over in their usual nine, honking off the beat, and as they crossed his line they fell for a few wingbeats into a perfect square, three by three, and honked once in perfect time. They seemed embarrassed by it. They loosened back into their swing and did not mention it again. No one else was on any of it. A day without people, Boof found, was not empty. It was only quiet enough to hear the land at work. At the top of the rise the light went long and gold, and then it went out all at once, the way a lamp is put out by someone with somewhere to be.

entries.label: Friday
entries.text: It was Friday before Boof had finished blinking. Below the rise, in the farms along the road, latches lifted. Smoke stood up from three chimneys at once. A bucket knocked a well and somebody swore at the cold — cheerfully, the way a person swears who has slept well and expects a perfectly ordinary day. Not one of them had missed anything. A Thursday is very easy not to miss, if nobody tells you it was there. Up the Bonk City road came a cart drawn by a mule in a knitted ear-cap, and on the cart a bell, and behind the bell a crier in a coat with too many buttons, ringing at every gate as if each gate had asked her to personally. “By leave of the table,” she called, “and the pie at the head of it! The remainder has come due!” Boof sat down in the middle of the road, so that the cart would have to stop or go around. It stopped. Carts usually did. The crier read from a sheet that had been folded so many times it was more crease than paper. At the Turning of the Year, in Bonk City, at the Feast of the Uneven Slice, the one destined to spill exactly one pie would come to the table. Not one pie and a bit. Not most of one. One. It had been foretold for so long that the city had stopped believing it — which was, the crier said, lowering the sheet, apparently the sign. Boof put her nose to the sheet where its corner hung over the rail. Ink, crease-dust, mule. And in the deepest fold, faint as a thumbprint, something cold and plum-dark that she knew from the hedge-bottoms at home, where baneberries drop and say things, and nobody steps on them in time. Then the last line, read slower: any household that has received a stranger without a receipt is asked to send word. She looked down over the rail at Boof. “Anything turn up at yours?” Boof looked across the road. The hat hung above the long grass at the verge, at the height of a person's head. Under it stood the figure, plain as chalk on slate, facing the hedge. The crier followed her look. “Oh,” she said. “Someone's put up a scarecrow. Not a very good one.” She regarded it with the generous eye of a woman who had seen a great many scarecrows and liked most of them. “Nice hat.” The figure turned his head. It did not turn the way a head turns. One moment the circle faced the hedge; the next it faced the crier, with nothing in between, and two dots in it. The crier, to her credit, did not drop the bell. She took out a pencil instead, and a clean slip, and held the one over the other for some time. Writing down what had arrived was her whole work. The maps took ink these days. There was no reason on earth it should not be easy. “I'll put that I saw a hat,” she said at last, and wrote it, and the ink stayed.

entries.label: Boof · The cart went on…
entries.text: The cart went on toward Bonk City with its bell, and the road went with it, in its usual bends. The figure went a quarter turn off the road, straight into the field. Boof sat in the road with the warm slice in her teeth and did the arithmetic a dog does, which is not done in numbers. The road was going to the feast. Everyone on it would be going to the feast. The feast was where the story was plainly meant to happen. The figure was going somewhere the story had not said. She could not smell him. She could smell that someone was. Far behind her, in the warm furrow, one ant-street ran perfectly straight, and at the end of it burned a torch that had been, until that morning, a little of somebody's arm. Boof went into the field.

entries.label: Labyrinth · Bonk City has no…
entries.text: Bonk City has no straight streets. Its lanes curl like the inside of a shell. Its bronze posts lean together to talk. Every road into it bends at least twice on the way in, so that whichever gate you came by, you arrive facing the plaza and the pie; the city likes to see your face. A straight line across Boon.land, then, does not come out at any gate the roads know. It comes out at the back wall, low down, at the parcel gate — the door the city takes its flour through, and its lamp-oil and letters, and anything else that comes in a box. Boof reached it at dusk, two days of straight walking after the hedge, with the sky behind her gone the green-black of a bruise on a pear. A storm was coming over the far hills, turning things over to see what was underneath. Every pane of glass in the back lanes had begun to hum, the way Bonk glass does when weather is coming. It remembers being struck, and would rather not be again. Pane-snails had clamped themselves flat to the humming glass. The lamplighters were out early, lamp-ladders folded into staffs, lighting the dent-lanterns one dent-bright corner at a time. Round each new flame the remainder-moths began their laps, which never close: every circle comes round a little past where it began, so that no moth in Bonk City has ever landed on the same spot twice. Ahead of her, under the hat, the figure stopped at the gate. Behind him, at the corner of the lane, one bronze post stood perfectly upright. It had leaned for two hundred years. It was not leaning now.

entries.label: The Parcel Gate
entries.text: The porter was hauling the gate shut when they came. He was a broad man with a lantern on a hook at his belt and the face of someone who has been told by a great many storms exactly what they think of open gates. The parcel gate was hung for three porters and has had one for thirty years, because of the storm-weight: an iron counterweight the size of a bread-oven, riding in a slot in the wall, that lets one man lift what three were meant to. Outside the wall, on the cobbles, stood the evening's last deliveries: crates of lamp-glass, a barrel of oil, and eleven sacks of fine flour stamped for the Feast of the Uneven Slice. There was time to shut the gate or time to bring the goods in. There was not time for both. He had chosen the gate. A Bonk City gate left open in a storm lets the wind into the lanes, and the wind in the lanes breaks glass, and the glass of Bonk City is made of every blow the city has ever taken. It does not like to take another. The bonk-kiln, which forgives old blows into new glass, is booked until spring. The figure was crouched in the gateway — folded, rather, at the middle, the way a line folds — over something small on the stones. The parcel gate is low. It was built for boxes. The figure fit under its lintel with room to spare. The hat did not. It hung at its usual distance above his head, and that distance put it exactly against the face of the stone. “Hat off, son,” said the porter. “Gate's coming down.” The figure looked up at the gap between his head and his hat — the gap already doing, as far as anyone could tell, precisely what the porter asked. The porter looked at the gap too. He looked at the sky. The first big drops came down on the flour sacks with a sound like someone knocking politely on a row of doors. Along the wall the chime-gutters began to ring, roof by roof, telling the city which of its roofs leaked. He had kept that gate thirty years by one rule: the gate comes down before the storm does. It was a good rule. He had seen what happened to the lanes the year somebody forgot it. He held the gate up anyway. The storm-weight took most of it; he took the rest with both hands and his shoulder, and in a wind the rest is plenty. Up in the slot, the gate-pigeons who sleep on the weight every night rode it an inch up and an inch down and did not wake. He said nothing, and the rain came down on the feast flour, and the figure went on with whatever he was doing on the stones. It took about as long as tying a boot. Then the figure straightened, all at once, with something in his hand, and stepped through. The hat did not come through the gate. It went over the wall instead, at its own height, without hurry, and came down on the far side at exactly the distance above his head where it belonged. The porter let the gate fall. The storm hit the outside of it a moment later, like a latecomer finding the door shut.

entries.label: Boof · Boof shook the rain…
entries.text: Boof shook the rain out of her ears and went to see what he was holding. It was a button: horn, a little scuffed, round, with two holes in it. Boof knew it. She had been under BoonWAP's table on the wet night somebody lost it, and had smelled the coat it came off, and had not thought of it once since. Lost things in Bonk City get kicked from lane to lane by the city's feet until they come to rest wherever nobody looks down. Nobody looks down at the parcel gate. He held it up to look at. Round, with two holes. For a moment Boof could not have said which of them was looking at the other. The porter, meanwhile, had gone out through the wicket into the rain and come back with the flour on his shoulders, a sack at a time, and stacked it by the lamp. Three sacks were spoiled through. The feast clerks keep a slip for this. DAMAGE, it says at the top, and under that, a line for the cause. Most porters write weather. It is nearly always true. He wrote his own name. Then he looked for a long moment at the figure, and at the hat, and at the dog, and said, “Right. I'll need to put you in the book.” Things that came through his gate went in the book. That was the whole of the world he was responsible for, and he had never once let it down.

entries.label: Record · That night the city…
entries.text: That night the city wrote him down three times. The porter wrote him in the gate-book, in the columns the gate-book has. Received: one, at dusk, by hand. Shape: rectangular, with handle (separate). Condition: dry, which was more than could be said for the flour. Sender: none. Receipt: none. Under remarks, after some thought, he wrote parcel. The carpenter came at midnight to look at the lintel, because the porter swore the hat had never touched it, and yet there was a mark on the stone: a curved line, faint as a fingernail's, exactly where something had very nearly touched. She ran her thumb along it and frowned. Then, since he was standing still, she measured him. Carpenters measure anything that stands still long enough. Her door-rule has a hinge for every size of door; she unfolded it against him, and it stopped on its own with a click, the way it does at any honest doorway. So tall. So wide. Square at every corner, with a line straight down the middle where a door would open. In her repair log she wrote: one door, standard, hung without frame. Opens — she held the pencil a while — inward. In the morning the night school's mistress found him at the back of her room. Her pupils, porters and lamplighters and laundresses who come after the day’s work to learn their letters, were practicing for the feast, as they did every winter, walking brass pie-dividers round paper pies to cut them into even slices for luck. Pie-dividers never come out even; the sliver left over is the luck. The mistress keeps the slivers in the sliver tin on her windowsill. Each winter’s slivers fill half the room the last winter left, so the tin is always filling and has never once been full. After pies came combines. Each pupil drew two nouns from a hat, chose a sigil and a container, and chalked them on the lid of a brace-box warmed between mittens. If the nouns agreed, the box fogged into a small weather. It teaches a pair of hands what will hold together before anything is built. Chalk is cheaper than oak, the mistress tells them, and a box that will not fog has cost nobody a beam. One laundress's {frost & hearth} snowed warm, and the front bench caught the hearth-drift on their tongues. A lamplighter's <river ~ moon> ran pale and would not stay. On the window the warm snow fogged the . face, the inside one; the # face, out to the lane, stayed clear. Above the slate, in the mistress’s round hand, stood the week’s copybook lines, to be copied ten times each before the brace-boxes came out: write it before you argue it; one shard at a time; keep the morning, not the week. The front bench had copied the first line ten times and was already arguing about the second. At the break the mistress passed round a bowl of boneberries off the vine over the parcel gate, where the flour carts brush it on the way in and the lantern-heat keeps the frost off. At the gate they taste of falafel: crisp at the skin, warm with cumin, soft and green at the heart. Pupils who had come straight from work ate three apiece and called it supper. Boof had the one the front bench dropped on purpose. The bowl went round once and came back empty, which is all a bowl of boneberries has ever promised. The figure was sitting on the end of the last bench with one line raised in the air, the way a pupil raises a hand, and nobody had called on him. She called on him. He did not say anything. She wrote him on her roll — one pupil, new, quiet, hand up — and left the space for his name blank, because you do not fill in anyone’s name for them. Three records. Each written by someone who had looked carefully and put down what they saw. Each one right.

entries.label: Three Receipts
entries.text: By breakfast the records office had all three, and the records office does not like a stranger to be three things. It sent for Mx. BoneWAP. BoneWAP came up from the lower town clean-boiled and exact, crust laid like a set of good joists, the listening mallet under one arm, and read the gate-book, and the repair log, and the roll, in that order — slowly, the way a builder reads a beam, not for what it says but for what it will bear. They tapped each once with the mallet's felt head, and listened. Then they pinned all three with brass rail-pins to the board in the hall where the city posts what has arrived: side by side, sources named, nothing smoothed into anything else. “Which is the true one?” asked a clerk. “Lean on any of them,” said BoneWAP, “and see if it holds.” They tapped the board. “A parcel is a thing someone is responsible for until it arrives. A door is a thing someone is responsible for keeping in good order. A pupil is both of those, for as long as the lessons take.” They stepped back. “I would not take any of them down. When the archive's glassing press has them, it can press all three, one over another.” “Glass over, never scrape,” said the clerk; everyone who has sat a winter at the night school has copied it. The clerk, who had a form with one box on it, went away to find a form with three. Before lunch the clerk had one, headed in a careful hand: [pupil, parcel, door]. A window of a form: three boxes to look into, none to stand in. Under the three, the clerk ruled one more box, smaller, with no heading at all. “A good form needs a box for what you do not know,” the clerk said, blotting it. “Left honestly open. Otherwise the next thing through the gate has to be cut down to fit the last.” BoneWAP tapped the empty box once with the felt head and listened. It held.

entries.label: Boof · None of which was…
entries.text: None of which was what the city was talking about. By noon the word had gone round every curve of Bonk City, as word does there, bouncing off the glass: the crier's notice had been right. Someone had come in at the parcel gate in the storm, and they had come with no receipt. By one o'clock the city had decided it was the dog. It made a great deal of sense, once you heard it. The dog had come in at the parcel gate. The dog had no receipt; dogs never do. The dog had been under the table, long ago, the night the button was lost — several people now remembered this clearly, including some who had not been there. And had the dog not once carried a slice of BoonWAP out of the plaza and never eaten it? That is not the act of an ordinary dog. That is a dog waiting for something. Boof smelled the idea going round before it reached her: cold at the bottom, plum-dark, the smell from the deepest fold of the crier's sheet. A foretelling said often enough comes true because it was said, and Bonk City bounces every word off its glass until it has been said a great many times. Nobody had stepped on this one. By now it was a great deal too big to step on. So they came for her, kindly, with a ribbon. They led her through the lanes to the plaza, where the pie was holding court, and where at the head of the long table the city had already set a second place, with a cloth, and a cup, and a plate, for the one who was coming. They sat her at it. The title of the one destined to spill exactly one pie settled on her the way a hat might, which is to say it did not quite touch. Boof looked at the plate. She looked at the cup. She looked at BoonWAP, warm and enormous at the head of the table, who looked back at her with the patience of a pie that has seen a great many destinies seated at that place and served every one of them. “Every destiny I have seated there has asked me the same question,” said BoonWAP, to the table at large. Nobody had asked him anything. “The answer is that the second place is not for whoever sits in it. It is for whoever it was set for. In my experience those are rarely the same guest.” He beamed at the full cup, very pleased to have been asked. At the edge of the plaza, by the washtubs, the figure stood a quarter turn away from all of it, watching the woman who was washing the plates.
